title: Shannon Airport shortlisted for major aviation industry award
excerpt: SHANNON Airport has been shortlisted for a major aviation industry award after being named a finalist in the Under 5 Million Passengers category at the Routes World Awards 2026.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Shannon Airport shortlisted for major aviation industry award
body: SHANNON Airport has been shortlisted for a major aviation industry award after being named a finalist in the Under 5 Million Passengers category at the Routes World Awards 2026.
The shortlist was announced this week by Routes, with Shannon recognised alongside airports from around the world.
The Routes World Awards recognise airports and other organisations for their work in developing air routes, building airline partnerships and supporting aviation connectivity.
Ray O’Driscoll, CEO of The Shannon Airport Group, said the nomination reflected the airport’s work to expand its network.
“We are delighted to be shortlisted for the Routes World Awards 2026,” he said.

“This recognition from the global route development community reflects the strength of the partnerships we have built with our airline customers and the commitment of our aviation development team to growing connectivity for the Mid-West and wider region.”
Mr O’Driscoll said Shannon currently has 40 routes, the highest number in 17 years, including five new routes to Madrid, Rome, Frankfurt, Warsaw and Poznan.
He said the nomination recognised efforts to attract new services and support route growth, benefiting tourism, business and the regional economy.

Airports shortlisted for the awards are assessed on criteria including route development strategy, marketing support for airline partners, innovation, commercial performance and initiatives designed to increase passenger traffic.
The winners will be announced at the Routes World Networking Evening in Frankfurt on October 22.

title: Clare autistic teenagers to showcase creativity at ‘Spectrum of Strength’ exhibition
excerpt: “SPECTRUM of strength” is the theme of this year’s Picture Voice Art Exhibition for autistic teenagers, a diverse and vibrant collection of artwork including tile mosaics, fabric pieces, blow paintings, spray paintings, photography, self-portraits and many other forms of creative expression.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Clare autistic teenagers to showcase creativity at ‘Spectrum of Strength’ exhibition
body: “SPECTRUM of strength” is the theme of this year’s Picture Voice Art Exhibition for autistic teenagers, a diverse and vibrant collection of artwork including tile mosaics, fabric pieces, blow paintings, spray paintings, photography, self-portraits and many other forms of creative expression.
The Exhibition will take place at 11.00am – 1.00pm on Saturday, 5th September 2026, in Room T117, off the An tSlí Corridor in the Tara Building at Mary Immaculate College, Limerick.

Approximately 30 teenagers from 12 secondary schools are taking part in the project. The participating Clare schools include Rice College Ennis, St. John Bosco Kildysart and St Anne's Killaloe as well as schools from Limerick, Galway, Tipperary & Dublin.

All entries will be displayed as part of the exhibition, with the ten pieces that best respond to the theme being professionally framed and given a more prominent position within the exhibition space. Every student who submits an entry will also receive a certificate of participation in recognition of their contribution.

Primary school teacher Jarlath Healy developed the method as part of his Masters in Special Education thesis. Speaking to The Clare Echo, the autism advisor for county Limerick highlighted the importance of giving autistic young people a voice in the Midwest.

“The students have all been invited to attend on the day, as they have been co-designers and collaborators in the development of the exhibition. This is a really important aspect of Picture Voice, as the project is about giving autistic young people a genuine voice and ensuring that they are actively involved in shaping the exhibition”.

“We will also have a guest speaker, Céira Moroney, a Consultant Speech and Language Therapist from Clare and is also autistic. One of the exhibiting artists, James Hynes Chadwick from Tipperary, will also be performing a song on the day. The event is free and the public are warmly invited to attend. It promises to be a really exciting and meaningful event ”, Healy continued.

title: Interest rises in one of a kind Kilkee church property
excerpt: ONE of Kilkee’s most recognisable buildings for almost two centuries, the former church could be yours with DNG.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Interest rises in one of a kind Kilkee church property
body: ONE of Kilkee’s most recognisable buildings for almost two centuries, the former church could be yours with DNG.

The unique four bedroom two bathroom property was originally constructed in 1845 and designed in a Gothic Revival style, characterised by its striking pointed-arched windows and dressed stone detailing.

Douglas Hurley, director at DNG O’Sullivan Hurley spoke to The Clare Echo about the extensive renovations recently undertaken at this one of a kind home. “The current owner bought it in 2017. He is a builder that specialises in restoration and doing up old buildings. He removed all the old floors and put in hardcore insulation and underfloor heating, new concrete floors throughout the building, new plumbing and new wiring”, Hurley explained.
“He recycled old materials such as the old seats that were used for some of the wall panelling. He tried to do it as sympathetically as possible to the work that was already there”, he continued.

As a result, the property’s impressive interior retains a wide variety of period features, including vaulted ceilings, original timber flooring, the original pulpit staircase, arched doorways and the original crafted timberwork, helping to effortlessly blend historical charm with modern living.

The property has unsurprisingly attracted a lot of attention due to its uniqueness and ideal location, just a short stroll from Kilkee's renowned horseshoe beach and vibrant seafront, while enjoying immediate access to the many amenities this popular coastal town has to offer.

“There’s been a lot of media interest. I suppose it’s quite unique and it’s quite quirky. It could be a home buyer or for people to use it as an Airbnb. It will be well able to accommodate large groups so there’s potential for very good income to come off it. It could be an investor looking for an Airbnb or a holiday home”, Hurley highlighted.
The property is for sale by online auction on Friday 04th September 2026 at 2pm (unless previously sold).

title: ‘West Clare is diminishing every day’ as calls grow for planning changes
excerpt: WEST Clare councillors have called for new national rural housing guidelines to be brought into effect as quickly as possible, amid concerns that current planning rules are contributing to the decline of rural communities.
author: Paige Foley
alt: ‘West Clare is diminishing every day’ as calls grow for planning changes
body: WEST Clare councillors have called for new national rural housing guidelines to be brought into effect as quickly as possible, amid concerns that current planning rules are contributing to the decline of rural communities.
The call was made at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District following a written notice of motion from Cathaoirleach Cllr Michael Shannon (FF).

The motion called on the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to ensure the Sustainable Rural and Gaeltacht Housing National Planning Statement is finalised and brought into effect no later than November 2026.

It also called on Clare County Council’s Chief Executive to ensure the Planning Department is prepared to implement the new statement, including how it will interact with the current Clare County Development Plan, rural settlement policies and Areas of Special Control.

In a written response, Senior Executive Planner Garreth Ruane said the recently published rural housing guidelines were still in draft form and would need to undergo Strategic Environmental Assessment and Appropriate Assessment.
It is understood the document will be finalised as a National Planning Statement following completion of the required statutory processes, with publication anticipated before the end of 2026.

Mr Ruane said Clare County Council would engage with the statutory process required under the Planning and Development Act 2024, in consultation with the Office of the Planning Regulator, once the finalised statement is published.

He added that while the council supports clear and consistent national guidance on rural housing, the timing of its finalisation rests with the Department and is subject to the completion of the required statutory processes.
Speaking at the meeting, Cllr Shannon said he had put forward the motion because he wanted to ensure there was “no delay in implementation”.
He said the new policy could take five or six months to come into effect but would ultimately have to be incorporated into the county development plan.
Cllr Shannon said depopulation was an issue across West Clare, pointing to local football teams having to amalgamate as one example.
He said the new policy would “not be a gamechanger for planning” but would make it easier for people to return to the parishes “where they were reared.”
Referring to his own parish of Quilty, he said it was “vital that this change comes in quickly”.
Cllr Dinny Gould (Independent), Leas-Chathaoirleach of the municipal district, seconded the motion. He said “West Clare is diminishing every day”, with people leaving the area for Limerick and Ennis.
Cllr Gould said some local communities “can’t even fill our football teams”, including in his own parish of Cooraclare.
Cllr Rita McInerney (FF) said she supported the motion and that a recommendation on planning policy was needed.

She said the issue was important for sustaining communities, particularly where people wanted to put down roots in the areas where they were raised or where they remained involved in local communities.

Cllr McInerney referred to a case involving a family member who had left land to a relative located around 800 metres outside a village boundary, saying planning was the issue despite all other aspects of the proposal being acceptable.
She said she hoped the new policy would help to “relax” some of the restrictions affecting such cases.
Cllr Shane Talty (FF) said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the proposed changes and welcomed the draft policy.
“We should be falling over ourselves to give people grants to come home from the United States and Australia,” he said.

He also referred to a case involving someone who had identified potential sites on ancestral land in West Clare but was unable to secure permission under the current policy because they had been “reared in Lahinch.”
Cllr Joe Killeen (FF) said anything that could increase the availability of housing should be welcomed, with greater success in securing planning permission favoured where appropriate.
He also raised the cost of additional assessments, saying these could be “really expensive” and difficult for young people to afford.

Director of Services Carmel Kirby said the draft guidelines had been finalised at national level but that the council would have to wait to see how they would ultimately be transposed into local authority guidelines.
She said the national process needed to be completed before the changes could be implemented locally.

title: Fitzgerald trained Tiermana Dream wins €20k Bar 1 sprint sweepstake for Clare syndicate
excerpt: Tiermana Dream winner of the BarOne national Irish sprint trained by Colm Fitzgerald and owned by the Zero Zero syndicate which consists of Nicholas O’Dwyer, Joe Kelly and Fitzgerald family members.
author: The Clare Echo
alt: Fitzgerald trained Tiermana Dream wins €20k Bar 1 sprint sweepstake for Clare syndicate
body: Tiermana Dream winner of the BarOne national Irish sprint trained by Colm Fitzgerald and owned by the Zero Zero syndicate which consists of Nicholas O’Dwyer, Joe Kelly and Fitzgerald family members.
YOUNG trainer, Colm Fitzgerald of Tullabrack, Kilrish landed the Bar 1 Sprint Sweepstake with Tiermana Dream Ireland claiming the €20,000 winner’s prize at Dundalk Greyhound Stadium.

In the country’s top competition for sprinting greyhounds, Tiermana Dream was first home. Owned by the Zero Zero Syndicate which comprises of Quilty’s Nicholas O Dwyer, Cooraclare native Joe Kelly along with Colm’s father and brother Michael and Liam, this fantastic greyound is a son of Ballyhimikin Jet and Tiermana Jetty and was bred by the late Noel Moroney from Mullagh. This latest win brings his earnings to just over €33,000.

The feature contest in last Friday night’s card at Galway Greyhound Stadium was the final of the Irish Retired Greyhound Trust A6 graded 525 Yards Stake with the concluding A2 graded contest the chief supporting affair.

As the traps rose for the I.R.G.T. A6 Stake Final Hazlehill Breeze Run For Mary and Drimeen Jetty were all prominent and as they raced towards the opening bend it was Hazlehill Breeze that led along the inner from Rallying Wild and with trouble behind the front pair kicked clear down the back. Racing past halfway Hazlehill Breeze led by three lengths but now the Stephen Murray of Sixmilebridge trained Run For Mary was beginning to find her stride and exiting the back straight she was taking dead aim at the leader and closing with every stride. Off the home bend Hazlehill Breeze still led by two lengths but the How-Deep-Is-It Syndicate of Sixmilebridge owned Run For Mary (Broadstrand Bono-Risky Reward) swept down the inner to take command close home to score snuggle by a lengths and three parts in 29.80.

Island Ivy and Slipalong Dew were both away well in the A5 graded contest and racing towards the opening bend Island Ivy held a narrow advantage over Ballyea Marshall with Knockdrum Sparky moving through along the inner and giving Ballyea Marshall a nudge that allowed him turn down the back in second place three lengths adrift of the pace setting Island Ivy. Racing down the back the Paddy and John Collins of owned Knockdrum Sparky continued to close on the leader as Ballyea Marshall got back on terms out wide. Taking the third bend, Knockdrum Sparky moved through on the leaders inner and striking the front on the crown of the home bend the son of Orchestrate and Highview Honour eased away to defeat the staying on Paradise Prada by two and a half lengths in 29.40.

In the early strides of the A6 graded 525 yards contest the Frank Casey of Newmarket-on-Fergus owned Pronto Bucks showed good early dash to lead on the run towards the opening bed from Kilbeacanty Lass with Lakeside Teagan, a length off that pair as they negotiated the opening bend. Turning down the back Pronto Bucks moved on by two lengths from Kilabeacanty Lass at as they reached halfway the lead had grown to four lengths as Confused Dexter came through to give chase from the rear. Between the final two bends Confused Dexter briefly looked a threat but Pronto Bucks (Burgess Bucks & Churchtown Minee) edged in again in the straight to score by a length and a half in 29.68.

The S3 graded sixth contest looked an extremely tight contest with the winners of fifty races heading to traps and little separating them on the clock and as the lids rose Light And Leafy was first to emerge and racing towards the opening bend he showed good pace to lead from old rivals Ballyea Jet on his outer ad Nashville along the inner. Approaching the turn Light And Leafy led by a length but as they rounded the bend the Noel Gavin of Ballyea owned Ballyea Jet loomed up on the leaders outside to eyeball his rival. Off the home bend Ballyea Jet (Jaytee Jet & Seekers Vision) struck the front and the Albert Mullins of Gort trained runner settled the contest in a matter of strides as she registered career win number eighteen by four and a half lengths from Colossal Journey in 19.21.

title: O'Connors treat customers on 65th birthday
excerpt: Loyal customers, dedicated staff and a strong work ethic passed down through generations are the key ingredients in making O’Connor’s Bakery a sweet success, says Ann Marie O’Connor, daughter of the original founders Pat and Mary, as the Clare institution celebrates 65 years in business.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: O'Connors treat customers on 65th birthday
body: Loyal customers, dedicated staff and a strong work ethic passed down through generations are the key ingredients in making O’Connor’s Bakery a sweet success, says Ann Marie O’Connor, daughter of the original founders Pat and Mary, as the Clare institution celebrates 65 years in business.

Established in 1961 at its original Parnell Street location in Ennis, O’Connor’s Bakery has now grown to eight shops across Clare, Limerick and Galway and is renowned for its premium quality confectionery and friendly service.
Recalling the early days, Ann Marie explained that her parents met in Kilkee before her father secured a job at Shannon Airport.
“After they got married, they were in Limerick for about a year while they looked for a place to open their business,” she explained.
“Dad kept his job in Shannon for a few years after the business opened. He baked at night, went to work, and then baked again when he came home,” Ann Marie reflected.
The bakery originally operated with a turf oven, producing a small range of traditional products including bread, tarts and shortbread.
“It was a small, simple beginning,” Ann Marie recalled, adding that family members played an important role from the outset.
“My mother’s uncle helped make the trays to put products on in the shop. Family was always a big part of it, and even my father’s brothers helped in the bakery at the time,” Ann Marie continued.
From this humble beginning on Parnell Street, the business expanded to O’Connell Street before eventually growing to eight shops.
While the business has grown significantly, one thing that has remained central to O’Connor’s is its strong connection with customers.

“There are a lot of characters who come in, and many don't just come for the bread; they come for the chat as much as anything else. That is what makes us different from supermarkets and bigger stores. It is on par with the product,” said Ann Marie.
The bakery also continues to produce a number of traditional products that have been enjoyed by generations of customers and remain an important part of its heritage.

However, Ann Marie emphasises that while the business is proud of its history and traditions, it is equally focused on moving forward, embracing new ideas and adapting to the changing needs of its customers.
“You must try to change and bring out new products as tastes change or as new trends come on the market. If there's an interest in something, you try it,” she explained.
The bakery’s dedicated staff have also played a major role in its longevity, with some employees having been with the company for more than four decades.
“We have some amazing people and the key to our success is our staff. Without them, we wouldn’t have a business. It’s not about any one person,” Ann Marie outlined.
Looking ahead, Ann Marie says the focus remains firmly on maintaining the high standards that have been at the heart of the bakery’s success for more than six decades.
At the same time, the company continues to invest in its future, having recently revamped its Gort shop and offering an online click-and-collect service.
Designed with busy families in mind, the service offers customers a more convenient and flexible way to order, helping them save time while still enjoying the bakery’s much-loved products.

title: New proposal seeks greater role for Kilrush students in local decision-making
excerpt: YOUNG people in Kilrush could be given a greater say in shaping the future of their town under a new proposal supported by Clare County Council.
author: Paige Foley
alt: New proposal seeks greater role for Kilrush students in local decision-making
body: YOUNG people in Kilrush could be given a greater say in shaping the future of their town under a new proposal supported by Clare County Council.

The motion, tabled by Cllr Ian Lynch (IND) at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District, calls for the reintroduction of annual civic engagement meetings with primary and secondary schools across the district.

It also proposes that the municipal district work with the Kilrush Town Team, local schools and student councils to establish an ongoing programme of consultation, allowing young people to contribute to future planning, development and regeneration projects.
Introducing the motion, Cllr Lynch said it was inspired by a conversation with an eight-year-old member of a school student council who approached him about changes made to a local playground.

He said the encounter highlighted the value of involving young people in local decision-making and questioned whether the municipal district could do more to bring children back into the conversation.
Cllr Lynch explained the initiative would help keep local democracy alive while encouraging civic pride and active citizenship among younger generations.
Seconding the motion, Cllr Rita McInerney (FF) said young people had “great ideas” and often knew exactly what they wanted and needed when issues directly affected them.

She added that Kilrush already had excellent youth workers and suggested existing national and international programmes could provide a framework for the initiative, meaning the council would not have to “reinvent the wheel”.

Cllr Gabriel Keating (FG) recalled inviting school groups into the council chamber during his early years as a councillor, describing it as a “fantastic” initiative that generated strong interest before it fell off the radar during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Senior Executive Officer John O'Malley said previous engagement through the Town Centre First programme had demonstrated how enthusiastic young people were when given the opportunity to contribute, describing it as “great learning”.

In a written response, Mr O'Malley said the West Clare Municipal District supported the proposal in principle and recognised the importance of providing meaningful opportunities for young people to engage in the civic, social and economic development of Kilrush and the wider West Clare area.

He said previous initiatives, including the Town Centre First process, the Mars Cinema regeneration project and other community programmes, had demonstrated the value of involving young people in discussions on the future of their town.

Mr O'Malley said the Kilrush Town Team provided an established forum through which engagement with young people could be further developed, working alongside schools, student councils, youth organisations and community groups.

He added that the proposal for an annual engagement meeting with primary and secondary schools was supported in principle and would be explored with Clare County Council, local schools and relevant stakeholders.
Cathaoirleach of the West Clare Municipal District, Cllr Michael Shannon (FF), said he would warmly welcome young people to attend MD meetings in Kilrush.
In concluding, Cllr Lynch said student councils in Kilrush schools had already shown they could make meaningful contributions, pointing to a recent school uniform change chosen by pupils themselves.
He said any future engagement should focus on issues relevant to young people rather than expecting them to sit through a full council meeting.
“If we're going to do it, make sure the community know we are there,” he said.

title: Scariff scare was Éire Óg's toughest test in two years – O'Connor
excerpt: ÉIRE Óg’s senior hurlers were challenged more than they had been in the last two years when surviving a second round scare with Scariff, manager Gerry O’Connor has said.
author: Eoin Brennan
alt: Scariff scare was Éire Óg's toughest test in two years – O'Connor
body: ÉIRE Óg’s senior hurlers were challenged more than they had been in the last two years when surviving a second round scare with Scariff, manager Gerry O’Connor has said.
Two wins from two outings has Éire Óg sitting top of Group 2 in the Clare SHC ahead of this weekend’s final round.

Though in a healthy position so far as scoring difference is concerned, Éire Óg have the unlikely scenario of missing out on the quarter-finals if they lose to Broadford and Crusheen overcome Scariff in round three.

County champions last year for the first time since 1990 and beaten at the quarter-final stage in 2025, O’Connor admitted their round two tie with Scariff was their toughest test over the past two seasons. “The reality is that Scariff brought a performance that probably we didn’t see coming and as a result we were certainly challenged more than we’ve ever been challenged over the last two years. We really struggled to deal with their puck-out, particularly the long direct ones. Patrick Crotty, Rossa Keehan and Keelan Hartigan in their half-forward line had us in all sorts of trouble and they were able to get vital possession to keep them in the game”.

O’Connor felt the introductions of Tom Kavanagh and James O’Dwyer had a big bearing in their seven point turnaround as they prevailed 2-20 1-21. “The bottom line is that we did eventually turn the tide and there were a few significant factors in that as they [Scariff] probably suffered a few injuries in the last quarter and probably making changes out of necessity whereas we were able to bring on tactical subs to be able to impact the game and that possibly stood us in good stead. I mean the points that Tom Kavanagh and James O’Dwyer got when we were five points down were huge and meant that the goal when it came had a greater impact in that vital last five or six minutes”.

He told The Clare Echo, “Overall we were just relieved as it was probably the toughest game that I’ve endured on the line in terms of trying to impact the game from the sideline and we were at the mercy of the subs and the impact that they could made as we were just trying to make something stick in order to get a foothold on the game. It wasn’t until we could get a handle on their long puck-outs that we started to finally motor and if anything the better team probably lost in terms of how well Scariff played and that’s genuinely the way we felt about it.

“We were delighted with the result of course but very disappointed with some aspects of our performance as for the majority our half-back line were dominated by their half-forward line. So we need to have a look at that and improve as we can expect another huge battle from Broadford the next day”.

body: DROIM RIASC offers an exciting new housing development in the heart of Tulla, offering a mix of high-quality two, three and four bedroom terrace, semi-detached and detached homes.

title: Clare TD criticises 'eulogising and heaping praise on thugs' following fatal M9 collision
excerpt: A CLARE politician has come under fire for labelling the teenage boys who died in the fatal M9 collision as “thugs”.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Clare TD criticises 'eulogising and heaping praise on thugs' following fatal M9 collision
body: A CLARE politician has come under fire for labelling the teenage boys who died in the fatal M9 collision as “thugs”.
Clare Fianna Fáil TD Cathal Crowe criticised some of the online reaction to a fatal collision on the M9 in County Kildare, saying he is concerned about the “glamourising” of dangerous driving online.
In a post shared to his Facebook page on Monday, August 17, Mr Crowe said he was “sick of seeing people eulogising and heaping praise on thugs”.
“Our sympathies and concerns should be for victims,” he said, adding, “Our support should be for An Garda Síochána.”

The post came after a fatal collision at Moone in Co Kildare on the M9 northbound at Junction 3 at around 3am on Sunday, August 16. Five teenage boys died after the vehicle they were travelling in the wrong direction on the motorway collided with a second car.
The second vehicle contained three women, two aged in their 30s and one in her 20s, and a seven-year-old boy. All four were taken to hospital with serious injuries.
Mr Crowe's Facebook post attracted thousands of reactions and hundreds of comments before the comments were later limited.
Speaking to The Clare Echo, Mr Crowe said he had sympathy for the families of those who died, but said his concern was with what he had seen online following the collision.

“I don’t like what I have seen online over the past 48 hours where a lot of young people are eulogising these five people and portraying them as heroes and glamourising this type of dangerous driving and that’s primarily what my post related to,” he said.
Mr Crowe said his primary concern was for the three women and seven-year-old boy who were seriously injured and hoped they would recover.
He said he had also viewed a series of TikTok videos involving dangerous driving.

“They’re not fatal incidents – and not all of them result in accidents – but I have seen far too many of these videos online, where people are challenging each other or are glamourising this type of driving and it’s absolutely reckless,” he said.
Asked whether he would change the wording of his original post, including his use of the word “thugs”, Mr Crowe said: “I don’t think we should be sugarcoating what has happened here in any way.”
He also called for a “more aggressive approach to road safety”, including training and possible future legislation to give Gardaí greater powers to take affirmative action.
The post prompted a mixed response online, with some commenters criticising Mr Crowe’s wording while others supported his position.

One commenter described it as “an unbelievable post from a TD”, saying the five teenagers were “sons, brothers, grandsons and nephews to heartbroken families” and urging people not to be “so quick to judge”.
Another commenter said: “100% agree… thoughts also go to the emergency services staff of Ambulance and Fire Services that have to deal with these accident scenes.”
At the time of publication, the post remains live on Mr Crowe’s Facebook page.

title: CAMOGIE: Winning starts for Inamona, Truagh/Clonlara, Scariff/Ogonnelloe & Newmarket-on-Fergus
excerpt: REIGNING champions Inagh/Kilnamona began their Clare Credit Unions Senior Camogie championship with a victory, as did Truagh/Clonlara, Scariff/Ogonnelloe and Newmarket-on-Fergus.
author: Gearóid Howley
alt: CAMOGIE: Winning starts for Inamona, Truagh/Clonlara, Scariff/Ogonnelloe & Newmarket-on-Fergus
body: REIGNING champions Inagh/Kilnamona began their Clare Credit Unions Senior Camogie championship with a victory, as did Truagh/Clonlara, Scariff/Ogonnelloe and Newmarket-on-Fergus.

Inagh/Kilnamoan comfortably accounted for newly promoted Clooney/Quin while two of their closest contenders, Truagh/Clonlara and Scariff/Ogonneloe also produced impressive opening day displays overcoming Feakle/Killanena and Tulla respectively.
Newmarket-on-Fergus withstood a cagey opening quarter with Clarecastle/Ballyea before going on to record a nine point win.
Inagh/Kilnamona 1-26 Clooney/Quin 1-02 Venue: Kilmaley
Just like they began their championship winning run last season, Inagh/Kilnamona started with a comprehensive victory to get their campaign up and running.

Clooney/Quin struck for the first green flag of the game inside the opening quarter through Emma Deegan, before Andrea O’Keeffe responded with a major of her own ten minutes later. As the sides headed for the dressing room the reigning county champions held a 1-13 to 1-2 lead.

Clooney/Quin, who earned promotion back to the top tier last year, played with the aid of the breeze in the opening half but failed to score against it after the interval with Inagh/Kilnamona showcasing a clinic of long-range shooting notching a further thirteen second-half points.

Centre-forward Andrea O’Keeffe was the star of the show for the winners, finishing with a personal tally of 1-6, all of that from play. The margin would have been greater, had former Clare captain Deirdre Murphy not pulled off some saves over the hour.

Newmarket-on-Fergus 1-14 Clarecastle/Ballyea 0-8 Venue: Fr McNamara Park, Doora
An Aoibhe O’Leary goal on nineteen minutes was a big moment as Newmarket-on-Fergus as they kicked off their senior championship campaign with a merited nine point victory over Clarecastle/Ballyea.

Magpies may have spoken in the lead-up to the tie about the Blue and Gold of Newmarket-on-Fergus always sending a shiver down Clarecastle’s spine but if truth be told, the historic rivalry that has existed on the hurling field has rarely extended to the camogie sphere, simply because Newmarket-on-Fergus have tended to be operating at a higher level to their neighbours.
Matters were evenly matched in the first quarter and the sides were tied on three occasions before O’Leary’s goal put a bit of daylight between them.

Evie Scanlan with a brace of frees had Clarecastle/Ballyea two points clear by the third minute before Emma Crowe opened Newmarket-on-Fergus’ account. Scanlan replied with another free but it was matched by an Ellen Casey effort and Crowe’s second to level matters for the first time.
Points from O’Leary and Annmarie Hayes nudged Newmarket in front for the first time on seventeen minutes, a brief lead with Scanlan replying from another placed ball.
Then O’Leary stepped up with the major and the Blues kicked on with three Ellen Casey frees in a row to hold a 1-8 0-6 lead by the sounding of the half time whistle.
On the restart, Newmarket-on-Fergus remained in control, Clarecastle/Ballyea’s confidence took a dip when Scanlan missed their first free of the half.

Geraldine O’Grady’s side kept the scoreboard ticking and outscored Clarecastle/Ballyea 0-6 0-2 in the second half to help to alleviate relegation worries but also give their hopes of progressing to the semi-finals a lift.

Newmarket-on-Fergus had good displays from goalkeeper Emma Jones, Laura-Mae Hannon and Caoimhe Lally in defence, Emma Crowe and Ellen Casey were lively around midfield with Laura McMahon, Aoibhe O’Leary and Kaci Toomey to the fore up front.

title: Ennis' Ben Lyne says no to Three Lions and answers Ireland's call
excerpt: ENNIS’ Ben Lyne has turned down England and has nailed his colours to the mast in wanting to line out for the Republic of Ireland.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Ennis' Ben Lyne says no to Three Lions and answers Ireland's call
body: ENNIS’ Ben Lyne has turned down England and has nailed his colours to the mast in wanting to line out for the Republic of Ireland.
Ben rejected a call to represent the England U16 squad and instead captained the Irish U15s this week where they faced Cyprus in the first of a double-header of international friendlies.

Currently part of the Manchester United academy, Ben is expected to feature for the clubs U18 side this year, they are managed by former club midfielder Darren Fletcher. Fellow Irish wingers, Shea Lacey and JJ Gabriel have stood out for the U18s under Fletcher.

Ex Man Utd youths coach, Neil Ryan had selected Ben for their upcoming U16 games against Italy in Florence but Lyne was quick to inform management he did not wish to be part of their plans, he withdrew alongside Emmanuel Famokun, they were replaced by Jaice Dore and Eliah Semakula.
In March, Ben made his debut for the Irish U15s scoring two goals in their 4-2 defeat to the Netherlands.

Last October, Ben was called up to the English U15s ID camp but his desire has always been to represent the Republic of Ireland and when the call to join the national U15 squad arrived, he duly answered. His decision to decline the England U16 squad comes as little surprise.

Ben signed for Manchester United last August from Wolves when several Premier League clubs were eyeing up the promising attacker. While Brexit rules have prevented many young Irish footballers from signing with clubs in the UK until they turn eighteen, Ben has been able to navigate over this obstacle through the fact he was born in the Cayman Islands.
A son of Seán and Maeve, Ben joined Wolves from the Cayman Islands football academy, Total Soccer Cayman, where he caught the attention of Wolves scouts in an English youth tournament.

Manchester United was in flying form for Manchester United in the recent SuperCup NI, helping them to win the Globe title in July where they defeated Tigres in the final. They came from a goal down with Lyne landing the equaliser and then struck a penalty to the back of the net in the shootout.

Lyne was the only Manchester United player to score in every match he started throughout the tournament, putting everyone on notice with a string of outstanding performances. His movement, composure and eye for goal were exemplary, he looked at home on one of youth football’s biggest stages.

title: Master craftsman John Torpey brought passion & pride to everything he did
excerpt: KILKISHEN’s John Torpey one of the county’s most eminent entrepreneurs will be laid to rest this week but leaves behind a lasting legacy that will transcend generations.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Master craftsman John Torpey brought passion & pride to everything he did
body: KILKISHEN’s John Torpey one of the county’s most eminent entrepreneurs will be laid to rest this week but leaves behind a lasting legacy that will transcend generations.
Torpey Hurleys founded by John in 1981 has become one of Ireland’s most respected and trusted brands with their hurleys used all over the world.

‘Passion & Pride’ may have been the title for the 2005 biography of one of John’s most loyal customers, Davy Fitzgerald but the two words were epitomised by John when it came to family, business, hurling and his community.

On Sunday, he died suddenly at the age of eighty four. Full of life and ideas, his death has shook those nearest and dearest to him, all who knew him adored his charisma and his grá for telling stories.

In May 1981, John applied for planning permission from Clare County Council to construct a hurley manufacturing workshop in Belvoir, Sixmilebridge. He received the green light later that year which led to the birth of one of the Clare’s most recognisable businesses. The idea had been simmering for some time and had placed an advert in the classifieds section of The Clare Champion publicly appealing for ash trees at the beginning of 1981. Further plans saw the addition of a new filter system in July 1996.

He grew up on the family farm in Kilkishen, after school he worked as a shop assistant at a hardware store in Ennis. From here, he moved to The Garden County and worked in the hardware business in Wicklow, his work brought him to Dundrum where he took responsibility for the timber department.

Home came calling and following the death of his father, John returned to East Clare to take over the family farm. His entrepreneurial spirit was beginning to emerge, he turned his hand from milking cows, growing cabbage and breeding collie dogs. He recalled in an 2014 interview, “I was doing whatever. could think of to make a few quid”.

On one damp winter day where he was prevented from doing much productive farm work, the penny dropped that he needed to find another way to supplement his farm income. He had always made his own hurleys while lining out with O’Callaghans Mills, Clare and Wicklow, he had a skill for it which led to Clare hurlers such as Ger Loughnane, Seán Stack, Seán Hehir and Enda O’Connor asking him to make their hurleys. “Over time too, I found that players were coming from further afield. The busier I got at making hurleys, the more I realised that I couldn't do that and the farming at the same time. So in 1981, I bought by my first woodturning lathe, set up a make-shift workshop and officially launched Torpey Hurleys on a full-time basis,” he recalled.

As a hurler, John was always prepared during his forty six year playing career. He would never arrive to a game with just one hurley, there was always a spare at the ready. He made his senior debut for the Mills at the age of fifteen and last lined out for The Fireballs aged 52 for the club’s junior team. His uncle Paddy gave him his first hurley and remembered decades later, “that was the day the first seeds were sown”.

Knowing the GAA’s benefits in networking and getting embedded in the community, he showcased his talents in Wicklow and won an All-Ireland junior hurling championship in 1967 and also won three Leinster titles with Wicklow.

O’Callaghans Mills were glad to welcome him home, he was trainer and goalkeeper of the 1968 side which won the Clare intermediate hurling championship which was their first adult title in thirty one years. He also received the call-up to wear the saffron and blue but was second choice goalkeeper to Éire Óg’s Paschal O’Brien and lined out with the county’s intermediates side. He ranked the 1977 Clare SHC final loss to Sixmilebridge as his biggest disappointment in hurling.

Goalkeepers need to have cat-like reflexes and John was also lively on his feet which was evident in his abilities as a set-dancer. In October 1982, he was involved in organising set-dancing classes for adults at the GAA pavilion in Kilkishen and won county and provincial set-dancing titles in Scór for O’Callaghans Mills.

Promoting Co Clare and its offering remained to the forefront of John’s mind. In March 1986, he was one of the leading organisers of a two-day visit of the Wicklow U16 hurling squad to Clare where they partook in a series of successful matches, sight-seeing tours and entertainment including a visit to Bunratty Castle & Folk Park.

Within the locality, John was involved with the Kilkishen Development Committee since its inception in 2011. He was one of the leading figures that helped to acquire the Cultural Centre through fundraising for the Kilkishen Church Restoration Project and was part of the personnel who participated in the Kilkishen Lord and Lady fundraiser from May to September 2012. He also had a hand in running Golf Classics, the raffle of a Ferguson 35 tractor and draws for All-Ireland final tickets.

Securing a consistent supply of good quality ash timber was one of the first challenges encountered by John when he set up Torpey. He was unable to find a consistent source in Ireland but luck intervened when he discovered a spot in the Netherlands where good ash existed. He flew there five times a year to personally select every tree from which their hurleys were made. “To make the curved head of a hurley which is capable of withstanding the force of other hurleys you need a curved grain. And this can only be found at the very bottom of the tree where the root turns into the base,” he previously explained.

Scór was the setting for his big break in 1982. While exhibiting hurleys at a competition in Millstreet, Co Cork, he met Joe Egan who was working as a buyer for a number of large retail stores, one of which was Arnotts. Within months, Torpey Hurlers were supplying Arnotts, their sports section is Elverys and Torpey has been a trusted supplier since 1982. Six months later, Lifestyle Sports came calling and over time, O’Neills, Heatons Sportsworld and independent stores became valued customers. “The best thing I ever did though was to put good quality hurleys into the shops,” he once stated.

Clare’s success in winning the 1995 All-Ireland SHC title proved to be the making of the business with stars like PJ O’Connell, Frank Lohan, Davy Fitzgerald, Brian Lohan, Fergie Tuohy, Conor Clancy and Ger ‘Sparrow’ O’Loughlin all using Torpey hurleys. “It was the makings of my business, it really was,” John told The Clare Echo in September 2020. He took immense satisfaction in seeing hurleys hold a Torpey in front of a sold-out Croke Park.

Famous faces have also got their hands on Torpey hurleys. When Barack Obama made his official State visit to Ireland in May 2011 and remarked, “you could say there’s always been a little green behind the red, white and blue”, he was presented with a Torpey hurley by then Taoiseach, Enda Kenny (FG). So too was Rory McIlroy at the 2014 Irish Open in Fota Island Resort.

During his time as Vice President of the People’s Republic of China, Xi Jinping met with John and received a Torpey hurler in Croke Park in what the Belvoir man called an “amazing” experience. The call came after he impressed doing workshops in Croke Park for the previous five years for the All-Ireland semi-finals and finals while the museum in Croke Park also showcased a video of John working with his old tools. The specially crafted hurley presented to Mr Zi was embossed by John’s daughter, Claire with the words ‘Croke Park Visit Ireland 19/2/12’.

From 2014, John was beginning to pass on the business to his son Seán who had returned from Loughborough University in the UK completing degree in Sport Technology while he had also worked for Adidas in Germany. At this time, the business had an annual turnover of €450,000, a staff count of eight and were manufacturing more than 70,000 hurleys per annum.

Sales revenue has spiked with the addition of their online store. The ability to see demand for their hurleys in Melbourne, Indianapolis, Germany, Canada, New Zealand and South Korea was a source of great pride for John. Before stepping back, he had set up a new business which made wood briquettes from the waste generated in hurley making, an enterprise which received funding from LEADER.

Advice for businesses was offered by John during a profile on him by The Sunday Independent in 2014. Knowing your business and product is key, he said, “You only get one chance to make a good impression, so be sure you know everything about your product so you can be confident when it comes to selling it”. Credit worthiness must be kept, he flagged, “Honour your commitments and develop a reputation for paying what you own. Then when things are difficult you are more likely to get the support you need”. His final piece of advice was that a bad tree bends with every wind, “you have to have a plan for your business and you have to work that plan. You can't allow yourself to always be swayed this way and that. Focus on quality and affordability”.

John will be sadly missed by his beloved wife Mary, his children Patricia, Pauline, Connie, Claire, Karol and Sean, his sons-in- law Tom, Jimmy, Michael, Shane and Brian, his daughter-in-law Michelle and his many grandchildren Aoife, Croídhe, Méabh, Gillian, Susan, Ella, Finn, Gwen, Pearse, Nichola, Emma, Paul, Jim, Faye and Robyn. He is also sadly missed by his brother Patrick, his sisters Margaret, Lena, Fran and Mary and his many nieces and nephews, brothers-in-law, sisters-in-law, extended family, neighbours and a wide circle of friends

title: Kilmaley must scale The Bridge to take top spot in Group 3
excerpt: KILMALEY have been on the standout teams in the Clare SHC but are well aware qualification to the quarter-finals “is not guaranteed yet” ahead of the final round of group games.
author: Seamus Hayes
alt: Kilmaley must scale The Bridge to take top spot in Group 3
body: KILMALEY have been on the standout teams in the Clare SHC but are well aware qualification to the quarter-finals “is not guaranteed yet” ahead of the final round of group games.

Scoring difference caught Kilmaley out in the 2024 group stages when a three point defeat to Cratloe, the winning score from Conor McGrath in the last act of the game put the South Clare through and sent Kilmaley packing.

That will be in their minds this weekend as they know a win is needed over Sixmilebridge to guarantee their advancement to the last eight when they clash in Cusack Park at 16:00 on Sunday. “Qualification is not guaranteed yet, We were n this position two years ago. Our aim is to take each game as it comes and next up for us is Sixmilebridge”.

For Culbert that pits him against his native club with whom he won Clare SHC titles as a player in 2000 and 2002 while serving as a coach and selector to the Bridge for their successes in 2013, 2015 and 2017 when current manager John O’Meara was in charge.
Back to back wins over Newmarket-on-Fergus and Wolfe Tones have Kilmaley on the brink of a successive quarter-final appearance. Culbert felt they used half-time to their advantage.

Only a point was between the sides at this stage but Kilmaley powered on to record a fourteen point victory. “In the first half Wolfe Tones didn’t let us perform like we did in the second half. We fixed a few things at half time and lads took a bit of responsibility for their position. We had to stop Rory Hayes hurling at wing back as he caused us a lot of problems,” Culbert outlined.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Brian said Conor Cleary’s goal early in the second half was a big turning point in the game. “They were hurting us when they had the ball and were carrying it. They are a good team and fellas really had to take responsibility, the scoring really doesn’t reflect the game. Conor Cleary’s goal gave us a bit more belief. The goals expertly worked”.

Daire Keane had an influential role in their first green flag with Culbert hailing his influence. “Daire is having some year. He is like a 19 year old, his fitness levels are phenomenal, he is a great leader. He took the chance and created the goal, that’s what you have to do and it was the right thing to do. Conor (Cleary) was very good inside, they did a good job on him in the first half but like the game aganst Newmarket, he stood up in the second half, won possession and gave the lead”.

Colm Killeen scored three points off the bench for Kilmaley, further underlining the depth at their disposal. “I had to tell a few lads that they weren’t starting..I knew we were going to get a reaction and get that performance from Colm (Killeen) when he came on because he is really learning and he is going to be a Kilmaley senior for the next ten years. We still have a few to come on and they are good complaints to have, we can change it around. It will add more to our game, it’s up to the lads to put their hands up and say they want to start”.

title: Doolin's distinctive heritage & legacy of Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire to be celebrated
excerpt: STORIES and the legacy of Doolin storyteller Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire will be celebrated in North Clare this week.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Doolin's distinctive heritage & legacy of Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire to be celebrated
body: STORIES and the legacy of Doolin storyteller Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire will be celebrated in North Clare this week.
Stiofáin’s stories will be brought back to life at a free event for over sixteens in Doolin Community Centre n Thursday (August 20th) at 19:30.

Local storytellers will take centre stage to celebrate storytelling, heritage and community. The evening is the culmination of a series of storytelling workshops facilitated by renowned storyteller and performer Aindrias de Staic of the Burren Storytelling Centre, with the assistance of Alysh Doyle and members of the Doolin Heritage Project.

During the workshops, local participants have explored the stories, characters, traditions and storytelling heritage of Doolin, learning how to bring this material to life for a modern audience. The event is funded by The Heritage Council and is supported by The Doolin Heritage Project.

At the heart of the project is the work and legacy of Stiofáin whose stories and knowledge form an important part of Doolin’s cultural heritage. Rather than simply preserving these stories as part of the past, the project gives a new generation the opportunity to explore them, learn from them and share them in their own voices.

Aindrias has worked with locals to develop their storytelling skills, helping them to transform material from Doolin’s rich oral tradition into a live performance. The result will be an evening where Doolin’s stories are told by local people, for the local community, while celebrating the storytelling tradition that has helped to give Doolin its distinctive cultural identity.

“This is about keeping the stories alive,” Andrias told The Clare Echo. “Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire behind a wealth of stories and a wonderful storytelling tradition. Through this project, those stories are being passed on to a new generation, giving local people the skills and confidence to bring them onto the stage and share them again”.

Born in Ballycullaun in December 1858, Stiffen attended school irregularly for two to three years, his parents Mícheál Ó hEalaoire and Cáit Ní Dhanachair were both storytellers. Like his father, he became a farmer and was involved locally with the Land League. He died on May 4th 1944 and never married. He became well known as a storyteller from around 1930, when the renowned folklorist James Delargy got to know him. Stories collected from him by Delargy were published in Daithí Ó hÓgáin (ed.), Leabhar Stiofáin Uí Ealaoire (Dublin, 1981). In addition, a good deal of material collected from him is housed in the National Folklore Collection, UCD, along with an account by him of his life, and an obituary by Seán Mac Mathúna.

title: Clare ICMSA warns of ‘frightening surge’ in farm accidents
excerpt: CLARE ICMSA chairperson Michael O’Dwyer has urged farmers to keep farm safety at the forefront of their work as a “frightening surge” in farm-related accidents and tragedies continues.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Clare ICMSA warns of ‘frightening surge’ in farm accidents
body: CLARE ICMSA chairperson Michael O’Dwyer has urged farmers to keep farm safety at the forefront of their work as a “frightening surge” in farm-related accidents and tragedies continues.

The Barefield farmer said farmers were working around the clock to ensure livestock had adequate water and feed supplies during challenging weather conditions, but warned that fatigue was becoming a growing concern.
“First and foremost, I want to express Clare ICMSA’s sincere sympathies to the families and friends of those who have tragically lost loved ones in farm accidents in recent times,” Mr O’Dwyer said.

“Many farmers have been working around the clock to keep water troughs filled and animals cared for during challenging weather conditions. Their commitment is unquestionable, but they also need to look after themselves.
“After a long and demanding spring, the respite of summer has not materialised, and fatigue is becoming a real concern on farms.”

Mr O’Dwyer, who is also a member of the ICMSA National Council, said the association had recently met with Age Action Ireland to discuss, among other issues, the high proportion of farm fatalities involving older farmers.
He said retired farmers had an important role to play in agriculture by sharing their experience and continuing to contribute, but stressed that farms must remain safe workplaces.

“Obviously there’s an important place for retired farmers to remain active on farms, sharing their experience and continuing to contribute. But first and foremost, farms must be safe and secure workplaces.
“Agriculture is a workplace, and we must always remember that.”
Mr O’Dwyer said agriculture continued to have one of the highest workplace fatality rates in the country.
There were 25 confirmed farm fatalities in 2025, accounting for almost 40% of all workplace-related fatalities in Ireland, he said.
“Those figures are deeply concerning and underline why safety must remain a priority every single day,” he said.
Farmers have also been urged to avail of financial supports available to improve safety on their farms.
Mr O’Dwyer said a 60% grant is available under TAMS for farm safety.
There is also a scheme for PTO shaft covers, providing 60% grant aid subject to a maximum eligible cost of €100 per cover for up to four covers.
In addition, the Accelerated Capital Allowances (ACA) Scheme allows farmers to write off 50% of the cost of eligible farm safety and adaptive equipment each year over a two-year period.
Mr O’Dwyer acknowledged the financial pressures facing farm families but said safety could not be allowed to become secondary.

“I fully appreciate that, for some farmers, simply putting food on the table for their families is the immediate priority. However, no matter how difficult things become, we cannot allow farm safety to slip.
“No job on the farm is so urgent that it cannot be done safely.”

title: Ennis women's rugby documentary to chronicle historic All-Ireland league debut season
excerpt: A DOCUMENTARY chronicling Ennis Women’s Rugby’s first season in the All-Ireland League will premiere on Thursday August 27th in the Old Ground Hotel in Ennis from 7pm.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Ennis women's rugby documentary to chronicle historic All-Ireland league debut season
body: A DOCUMENTARY chronicling Ennis Women’s Rugby’s first season in the All-Ireland League will premiere on Thursday August 27th in the Old Ground Hotel in Ennis from 7pm.
Ahead of the event, women’s head coach Gareth O’Hanlon spoke to The Clare Echo about the filming process and how the idea for “Who We Are – Ennis Rugby in the AIL”, came about.

O’Hanlon, who is entering his fifth season as head coach after taking charge when the women's team was first established, said the idea for the documentary came from James Lynch, a member of the popular ‘Intensive Clare’ sports podcast.
“We had a lot of the footage and he just said wouldn't it be cool to just document the first ever All-Ireland league team to play in the league”, O’Hanlon explained.

“James just started off by looking at the preseason and the gym sessions then pitch sessions after that he started interviewing players and coaches and filming the matches and talking about them as well”, the coach continued.

Winner of a Munster Schools Senior Cup with St. Munchin’s in 2006, the Limerick man played at junior and senior level for Richmond for a number of years before taking charge of the Ennis RFC women’s team in 2021.

O’Hanlon described the filming process as “seamless”, adding that with Lynch “For a lot of the time we wouldn’t even know he was there. I suppose it gave us an opportunity to kind of reflect week on week when we were sitting down with James and the players as well”.

“It just gave us an opportunity to reflect because it was such a busy year. Our first year in the All-Ireland League was extremely busy and it was all new to us. It was very enjoyable and it’s something that the players will have forever. They'll have that documentary to look back on and it's a big part of one, women's rugby history and two, the history of rugby in Clare as well. So it's a nice keepsake and a memory I'm sure a lot of them will remember forever”, he continued.
Initially, the players had “a mixed bag” of reactions to appearing on camera but O’Hanlon said that the squad ultimately came to enjoy the project.

“They were kind of worried but they enjoyed it. It was a way for them to voice how the experience was for them week on week as well. It was very enjoyable for a finish. I think the players are so excited to look back on the year because it's hard when you're kind of in it, it’s like a roller coaster. Now a couple of months on, I think they're only now starting to understand how successful last season was and they're looking forward to just watching it back and reliving a lot of the special memories they made throughout the season”, said O’Hanlon.

The film is being screened as part of a fundraiser for the team and players, coaches and the filmmakers will be there on the night. Kilrush RFC will also be in attendance, having played a significant role in the initial set up of the Ennis RFC women’s team as they initially played together in an amalgamation before being stopped from competing together as amalgamations are not allowed in the AIL.

“We're very excited and although we're moving on to a new chapter, moving on to season two, it's going to be nice just to sit down and reflect and try to get our head around last season and understand how successful it was”, O’Hanlon added.

title: Morey Movement strengthens Sixmilebridge community through fitness
excerpt: A SIXMILEBRIDGE gym founded by first cousins Seadna and Chloe Morey is continuing to grow as the village’s population expands, with the owners keen to provide an accessible space for people of all fitness levels.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Morey Movement strengthens Sixmilebridge community through fitness
body: A SIXMILEBRIDGE gym founded by first cousins Seadna and Chloe Morey is continuing to grow as the village’s population expands, with the owners keen to provide an accessible space for people of all fitness levels.

Established in 2021 by former decorated inter-county stars Chloe and Seadna Morey, Morey Movement identified a gap in the local community for a facility focused on conditioning and general fitness and has gone from strength to strength since then.

“We have a massive interest in strength and conditioning,” Seadna explains. “We just wanted to bring something to the community in regards to keeping health and fitness as a priority for people and giving them an outlet to be able to come and exercise”.

The cousins currently run a sports camp for children in Sixmilebridge and said the idea for the gym developed naturally from their involvement in the local community. They subsequently completed their qualifications with Setanta College while continuing to work in their previous jobs before opening the facility.

Morey Movement operates on a pod based system, where members have access to their own squat rack and bench and are free to work out at their own pace rather than sharing with others. The gym is used by the Clare senior hurlers and has a contract with Sixmilebridge GAA to provide strength and conditioning for underage members, as well as providing a space for locals just looking to keep fit, showcasing the wide range of services and coaching available.

Chloe says that providing amenities for new and existing residents was an important consideration following The Bridge’s recent growth. “When a village grows like that numbers-wise, it's important that there's amenities for them as well. We didn't just want a run-of-the-mill gym. We wanted to create a space where everybody's welcome”, she explains.

This unique approach allows exercises to be tailored to each person's ability and experience, Seadna outlines. “You could have never come into a gym before in your life and when you come in the coach on the day would ensure that every single exercise is detailed towards your technique, your ability and we slowly build you up from there”, the two time All-Ireland and five-time Clare SHC winner highlights.

The owners have also noticed a growing focus among members on strength and overall wellbeing rather than simply losing weight in recent years as Chloe points out that “People these days now are more conscious of actually gaining strength. It's not all about losing weight. More often now people are realising how brilliant strength work is for their head more than anything and the improvement in their mental wellbeing”.

For Seadna, some of the most rewarding aspects of running the gym come from seeing small changes in people's everyday lives. “You might have someone come over to you and say ‘I did this for the first time in my life’ or ‘I don't feel my back pain anymore. It's the small things. It's not the athlete who's been out running, winning a race or anything like that. It's the small little changes in people's lives that you hear the stories about that kind of make it rewarding”, the Sixmilebridge native notes.

Looking ahead, the cousins hope to strengthen their links with other businesses and organisations in the village through events and initiatives. For now however, Seadna believes there are still plenty of people in the expanding village who are unaware of the gym and is determined to continue their progress. “The village is so big, I don't think a lot of people still know we're actually really here. It might not be for everyone, but getting in the door is the hardest part for people”, he explains.

title: 'Inagh/Kilnamona are best team in this year's Clare SHC'- says Clonlara boss Madden ahead of crunch clash
excerpt: CLONLARA view their final round opponents Inagh/Kilnamona as the best team so far in this year’s Clare SHC.
author: Eoin Brennan
alt: 'Inagh/Kilnamona are best team in this year's Clare SHC'- says Clonlara boss Madden ahead of crunch clash
body: CLONLARA view their final round opponents Inagh/Kilnamona as the best team so far in this year’s Clare SHC.

2023 champions Clonlara need a win over Inagh/Kilnamona on Saturday (16:30) in Zimmer Biomet Páirc Chíosóg to qualify for the quarter-finals, a defeat coupled with a Ballyea win over St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield would eliminate the South-East Clare side from the championship.

Securing the necessary result against Inamona will be a tough ask, Clonlara manager Donal Madden stressed. “That won’t be easy though as I’ve seen most teams so far in the championship and Inagh/Kilnamona have been the best so far in my opinion so we know the task ahead”.

Late points from Ian Galvin and Aidan Moriarty managed to rescue a draw for Clonlara who trailed by two points in additional time against Ballyea a fortnight ago. “I know we equalised at the end but we feel it’s a point lost to be honest as we were very disappointed with our second half performance. We were in a really good position at half-time but we feel that in the second half we wasted a lot of ball, our work-rate was down, our tackling was down so we’re really disappointed”.

Donal felt Clonlara didn’t hit the levels they are capable of reaching. “The wind was tricky but even still we’re way better than that. We’ve too much effort and commitment put in to play like that so we’re just really gutted with that performance”.

He told The Clare Echo, “The guys did dug it out at the end and a point is better than none but we shouldn’t have been in that position to be honest as we hit too many wides, lost too many tackles and make too many mistakes. We had enough possession in the second half to be at least six or seven points up so we shouldn’t have really been in that position at the end. The positives are that we’re still in it and we could very well been out of it had things been different for a finish so we have to go the next day and get a result”.

title: Stopping military use of Shannon would damage Irish & US links says NATO commander
excerpt: RELATIONS between Ireland and the United States of America would be damaged if the US military was prevented from using Shannon Airport according to NATO’s top military commander.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Stopping military use of Shannon would damage Irish & US links says NATO commander
body: RELATIONS between Ireland and the United States of America would be damaged if the US military was prevented from using Shannon Airport according to NATO’s top military commander.
Significant security implications would arise if the US military lost access to the use of Shannon Airport, General Alexus Grynkewich has said.
Grynkewich is NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe and Commander of US European Command.

During his first visit to Ireland, General Grynkewich labelled Shannon Airport as “a very important logistics hub”. He said, “It allows America to project power and keep threats at bay from all over the world. I think there’s some significant security implications from losing access there. Would we be able to find somewhere else that we could use? Perhaps, but Ireland’s been a great partner by providing access there for years and that’s let us hold terrorist threats at bay, that’s helped us to stabilise Iraq and other places”.

Millions of US soldiers have passed through Shannon Airport over the past two decades as it transformed into a significant transit point for the US military, particularly for its operations in the Middle East. For the first six months of 2026, there has been a drop of 42 percent of US troops using Shannon Airport, figures from January 1st to the end of June show there have been 15,236 US troops flying through Shannon, down on the 26,340 from the same timeframe in 2025.

Monthly protest vigils are held by Shannonwatch in the airport town on the second Sunday of every month. The group of peace and human rights activists seek to end the US military’s use of Shannon Airport, to stop rendition flights through the airport, and to obtain accountability for both from the relevant Irish authorities and political leaders.

Between 2022 and 2024, nearly 2,000 US military aircraft and US civil air operators with declared munitions of war on-board applied for exemptions to stop in Ireland. The flights were frequently to and from Germany, Poland, Bulgaria and Kuwait.

These planes are not routinely searched or inspected by Irish authorities. Only 0.1% of applications from US civil aircraft were refused to land or fly over Ireland due to the “nature of the total munitions of war proposed to be carried”, the Department of Transport have said.

As the most westerly airport in Europe, Shannon is a strategic location. Shortly after it opened in 1945, Shannon Airport became a convenient transatlantic refuelling stop for US military and diplomatic flights.

Soviet carrier Aeroflot had established a base there, allowing flights from the Soviet Union to refuel in Ireland before travelling onwards to countries such as Cuba and Angola. Shannon became the biggest Soviet transit airport outside Moscow until the 1990s.

From the 1990s, there has been an increase in the US military using Shannon Airport, this is connected to Operation Desert Storm in the Gulf. Activity was ramped up further at the turn of the century when, following 9/11, Shannon Airport became a key transit hub for US troops travelling to Afghanistan and Iraq. The Irish government had offered the use of Shannon to the US government for landing and refuelling facilities after the terror attacks after a UN Security Council Resolution which requested states work together to bring to justice those responsible for 9/11.

In 2003, the Dáil voted to support the government’s policy of continuing to grant overflight and landing rights in Ireland to US military and civilian aircraft. Over ten years from 2001 to 2011, over two million US military personnel flew through Shannon Airport. 2005 was the busiest year when nearly 2,000 aircraft carrying 336,000 personnel flew through the airport.
Under the Air Navigation Order 1952, no foreign military aircraft is permitted to fly over, or land in the State without the 'express invitation or permission of the Minister’.

However, under the terms of a specific arrangement dating from 1959, US military aircraft can overfly without prior notification on condition they are unarmed, carry only cargo and passengers, and comply with navigational requirements. Permission must also be sought to land and take off in Ireland as long as there are no arms or munitions on board, no involvement in military exercises or operations originating in Ireland, and no intelligence gathering.

In 1993, General Grynkewich graduated from the United States Air Force Academy. During his career in the U.S. Air Force, Grynkewich was an F-16 Fighting Falcon and F-22 Raptor pilot, and has over 2,300 flight hours. His senior posts have included commander of the 53rd Wing and deputy commander for operations of the Operation Inherent Resolve Combined Joint Task Force, which was heavily involved in the war against the Islamic State.

Ongoing working relations between Ireland, the US and NATO are to the advantage of all parties, he said. “I would just use as evidence issues that we had with access and basing during recent operations in Iran – from a US perspective. That was very unhelpful and you’ve heard President (Donald) Trump say that”.

Asked on RTÉ if Ireland was regarded as a weak link in terms of protecting critical infrastructure at the edge of Europe, he commented, “I certainly think we all have an interest in making sure that they are appropriately defended. We have seen critical underwater infrastructure like that be attacked in other places through hybrid warfare, dragging an anchor across it, etc. As a military commander, some of my military communications go across those cables as well, so it becomes a real military concern of mine. “I would not use those types of terms because I think that impugns whether, ultimately, Irish sovereign decisions when it comes to its strategy of neutrality and its place in the world”.

title: Feakle Festival hits the high notes with 'biggest festival ever'
excerpt: FEAKLE experienced its biggest ever traditional music festival with over 10,000 visitors coming through East Clare to sample the craic and ceol.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Feakle Festival hits the high notes with 'biggest festival ever'
body: FEAKLE experienced its biggest ever traditional music festival with over 10,000 visitors coming through East Clare to sample the craic and ceol.
Held from Wednesday August 5th to Monday August 10th, the Feakle Festival hit the high notes with 250 campervans perched up in the East Clare village and its surrounds.
Organisers say the festival brought more than 10,000 people to East Clare and all events were sold out.

Over 400 people partook in the workshops as the Feakle Festival recorded its most successful week which also provided an economic boost to local businesses, particularly those in the hospitality and pub sector.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Cllr Pat Hayes (FF) who has had a lifelong involvement with the festival, commented, “this was the biggest festival ever, we were blessed with the weather. With the scramble for tickets for different events, people said it was a bit like Electric Picnic or trying to get tickets for an All-Ireland final”.

Hailing the 2026 festival as “a phenomenal success,” Cllr Hayes stated, “the economic value of the festival to Feakle, East Clare and the entire county is huge. The amount of people who flew in from all over the world, they came from Japan, England, Brussels and China to be here, to immerse themselves in East Clare. The celebration of the Tulla Ceili Band set the tone for the week, event after event was sold out from then on. The volume of people who stayed in houses, campervans, tents, 300 people stayed in campervans and tents outside of them staying in Ennis and Gort, it makes a huge return and keeps businesses afloat for whole year”.
With 2027 marking the 40th Feakle Festival, Cllr Hayes said the success “lays down a marker to have more programming and keep the uniqueness of the Feakle Festival”.

He continued, “Feakle is a living village, it is not a tourist village, it recreates itself for the week, it will never be Doolin, Westport or those places, it is uniqueness that it can keep recreate as a living village for the week. The regular sessions that take place in Peppers every Wednesday and Shortts every Thursday is what its about. People want to come back to where the music is from, a lot of people went to Belfast for a day or two of the Fleadh and then did the week in Feakle or the oppoisite, people didn’t want to miss it. The welcome really comes across, you are getting real Ireland, it isn’t commercial”.

On the clash with Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann, Cllr Hayes said, “It doesn’t affect us at all, a couple of years ago we thought about changing it but a lot of musicians aren’t into competitions or don’t travel to larger towns for Fleadhs. If we could bottle what is in Feakle, that is what people come for, the unique experience of Feakle doesn’t come close to a Fleadh, I am not taking from the Fleadh, it had one million visitors but there’s something special in Feakle”.

Eightieth anniversary celebrations for the Tulla Céilí Band and the launch of an anniversary CD kicked off the festival while ninety years of the Tulla Pipe Band were also celebrated. Tulla fiddler, Sorcha Costelloe took a look at the past and future in a presentation titled ‘Looking back while moving forward: The past, present and future of the East Clare Music Tradition’.

Workshops were held on Thursday, Friday and Saturday morning where the tutors included the iconic Martin Hayes, Mary McNamara, Claire Keville, Jack Talty, Terence O’Reilly, Nuala Kennedy and Páraic Mac Donnchadha, Sold-out concerts were a constant of the festival.
