title: 'We were by no means perfect' – Éire Óg ship three goals for first time since 2020
excerpt: ÉIRE ÓG have guaranteed their place in the Clare SFC quarter-finals for the tenth year in a row but have pinpointed getting quicker at their transition from defence to attack as a key area to work on.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: 'We were by no means perfect' – Éire Óg ship three goals for first time since 2020
body: ÉIRE ÓG have guaranteed their place in the Clare SFC quarter-finals for the tenth year in a row but have pinpointed getting quicker at their transition from defence to attack as a key area to work on.
Back to back wins over Cratloe (1-17 0-4) and Doonbeg (2-15 3-9) sealed the champions’ spot in the knockout stages after just two rounds.

Advancing to the last eight was the initial target for the Townies before they began the defence of the Jack Daly, manager Shane Daniels said. “I think it guarantees us a place in the quarter-finals which was our aim at the start to get to a quarter-final, we used our panel again today, we had guys to come on again. David Loftus made our first start for the club and did really well around the middle of the field, Danny Lyne came on and got a very important score, Fionnan Treacy came on for his first senior game and he is a fantastic footballer, we’re getting a serious squad which is brilliant”.

Doonbeg were the first Clare side since Kilmurry Ibrickane in the 2020 quarter-finals to put three goals past Éire Óg. “It is the first time in Clare that we’ve been caught for three goals in a long time, we’ll go back and look at the video to see. Sometimes you get caught for goals, it is how you react to them, they got two goals and we scored 1-1 so we had a good reply in the first half, we actually played okay against the breeze if you take the goals out of it which were well worked moves by Doonbeg, we had a lot of control on the game but we weren’t happy with conceding goals, no team is happy to concede goals,” the Clare SFC winning goalkeeper of 2022 and 2024 stated.

Mark McInerney’s goal on thirty eight minutes gave Éire Óg the lead for the first time against Doonbeg in what was a tough encounter for the Ennis side. “We came back to West Clare and got a tough battle but we expected it, we were saying it all week that Doonbeg would come with fight, they are a good up and coming young side, they have a lot of work done and they had a decent game plan, it took us a while to figure it out, we struggled at times and we weren’t happy with a lot of aspects of our play but we got the job done in the end which is the main thing”.

Hunger and work ethic from the Townies’ forwards was central to them pulling things back in the second half. “It is one thing we demand all the time, we demand that our forwards work hard and if they don’t work hard they are no good to us, it is something that is one of our principles and that is what we expect”.

Daniels told The Clare Echo, “We’ve a lot to work on, our quick transition when we turn a team over, our control of the ball at times can be mixed, they tried something different and we expected it, it took us a bit longer than we thought to deal with it, we’ve defensive and attacking aspects that we need to work on, overall we’re delighted to get the result”.

St Joseph’s Miltown await in round three before Éire Óg zone in on the knockout stages but Shane insisted they have a lot to work on. “There was a small bit of a breeze in the second half which helped. Our message at half time was to keep doing what we were doing, keep working hard, making the right runs, try win the break when the ball drops, try move the ball as quick as we can, take the chances when they come, we had wides that we weren’t happy with but we have loads to work on, we were by no means perfect”.

title: Premier Powerwashing celebrates 4 years in business
excerpt: PREMIER Powerwashing Services is celebrating four years in operation after building a strong local reputation through repeat customers, recommendations and word of mouth.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Premier Powerwashing celebrates 4 years in business
body: PREMIER Powerwashing Services is celebrating four years in operation after building a strong local reputation through repeat customers, recommendations and word of mouth.
Since establishing the business in 2022, owner Brian McDonagh now provides exterior cleaning services to residential and commercial customers across County Clare and surrounding areas.

On the background to the business, Brian explains that “ Before becoming self-employed, I had worked in the industry and gained valuable experience, so I had a good understanding of the work, the equipment and, most importantly, what customers expect from a professional service”.

“I'm proudly local and Ennis-based, and I wanted to build a business that would provide a professional and reliable exterior cleaning service to people in my local community and throughout County Clare. I decided to take the step into self-employment because I wanted to build something of my own and have the opportunity to develop a business based on the standards and values that are important to me”, he continues.

Quality workmanship and customer service are central to the way the Ennis-based business operates, with the owner personally dealing with customers from the initial enquiry through to the completion of each job.

“I genuinely care about the quality of the work I do”, McDonagh said. “Because I'm the owner and the person carrying out the work, I take a lot of pride in every job I complete”. This mentality extends to Premier Powerwashing’s day to day operations as rather than rushing jobs, each property is assessed individually to determine the most suitable cleaning method for the particular surface.
Honesty and reliability are also key principles of Brian's fast growing enterprise, with customers given advice on whether a service is necessary and which approach would be most appropriate.

“I believe in being honest with customers from the beginning”, he explained. “If I don't think something needs cleaning, or if I think a particular method isn't suitable, I'll tell them”. Brian added that new customers can expect “good communication, honest advice, quality workmanship and someone who genuinely takes pride in the work”.

title: Section of Cliffs of Moher sea stack crashes into Atlantic
excerpt: A SECTION of the iconic An Branán Mór sea stack at the Cliffs of Moher has broken away and fallen into the Atlantic Ocean.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Section of Cliffs of Moher sea stack crashes into Atlantic
body: A SECTION of the iconic An Branán Mór sea stack at the Cliffs of Moher has broken away and fallen into the Atlantic Ocean.
The change to the 67-metre-high sea stack was spotted on Thursday, August 13, by Doolin Ferry captain Jim Griffin while operating a Cliffs of Moher cruise.
Captain Griffin said he immediately noticed the change after sailing past the sea stack, which is one of the most recognisable rock formations beneath the cliffs.
“We sail past the sea stack daily, so I immediately noticed that a substantial section had broken away,” he said.
“The rock formation was created by thousands of years of erosion, and that process is still happening before our eyes.”
Footage showing the newly eroded section was shared by Doolin Ferry on social media and has attracted approximately 3.4 million views across its various platforms, according to the company.
The rockfall occurred after the main seabird nesting season had ended. An Branán Mór and the surrounding cliffs provide nesting habitat for seabirds which return to the Cliffs of Moher each year.
Rockfalls are a natural part of the ongoing erosion of the Cliffs of Moher, with the coastline continually shaped by the Atlantic, wind and weather.
The cliffs were formed approximately 320 million years ago from sediments deposited by ancient rivers and later compressed into layers of sandstone, siltstone and shale.
An Branán Mór was originally connected to the main cliff face before being separated by coastal erosion over thousands of years.
The Cliffs of Moher stretch for approximately 14 kilometres along the Clare coast and reach around 214 metres at their highest point.

title: Tones tuned for 'monster game' with Newmarket-on-Fergus
excerpt: WOLFE TONES are braced for “a monster game” with neighbours Newmarket-on-Fergus which is expected to be one of the ties of action packed final round in the Clare SHC.
author: Seamus Hayes
alt: Tones tuned for 'monster game' with Newmarket-on-Fergus
body: WOLFE TONES are braced for “a monster game” with neighbours Newmarket-on-Fergus which is expected to be one of the ties of action packed final round in the Clare SHC.
Broadford will be the setting for the latest battle between the Tones and the Blues, Sunday’s tie commences at 16:00 in Glenomra Park.

Last season, Wolfe Tones powered past Newmarket-on-Fergus with a six point win to send their neighbours into a relegation play-off. Should the Tones emerge on top this weekend, they will once again have the Blues fighting for senior survival.
Not alone can they inflict some pain on their rivals but a win would more importantly see them advance to the quarter-finals if Kilmaley overcome Sixmilebridge.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Wolfe Tones manager, Barry Keane commented, “We just have to put our heads down now, we have a monster game, they don’t come any bigger. The prize is massive for both teams, Newmarket are going to be coming at us. They want to win, they are at the bottom of the table, they were very good the last day, they played better against Kimlaley than we did. We are just going to have to be up it another bit”.

Only a point separated Wolfe Tones from Kilmaley at half time in the second round but they conceded three goals in the third quarter before falling to a 3-20 0-15 loss. “We were really happy with how we played in the first half. We came out for the second half and missed three scores and conceded 2 succour goals. Kilmaley are excellent, they are one of the favourites for the championship for a reason;. We just couldn’t get back into our groove again in the second half. That third quarter was decisive. We have no complaints,” Keane reflected.

Barry who guided Wolfe Tones to Clare IHC success in 2024 added, “that third quarter wasn’t good enough from our perspective. We have to give Kilmaley the credit, they turned it on and we had no answers to it. The concession of goals is particularly disappointing from our perspective. We conceded three against the ‘Bridge and three again today. It’s something we have to look at”.

Focus switches entirely to Newmarket-on-Fergus, Keane stated. “That third quarter wasn’t good enough today and the lads know that, they just spoke about it and they don’t need me to tell them that. We will go again, the full focus now is on Newmarket. We will put the head down and go again”.

title: Planning sought for new Adult Day Services Hub in Shannon
excerpt: PLANS have been lodged for the change of use of a commercial building in Shannon to an Adult Day Services Hub operated by Enable Ireland Disability Services.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Planning sought for new Adult Day Services Hub in Shannon
body: PLANS have been lodged for the change of use of a commercial building in Shannon to an Adult Day Services Hub operated by Enable Ireland Disability Services.
The application, submitted to Clare County Council by Peter Scully of Enable Ireland Disability Services Ltd, relates to a building on the Link Road in Smithstown.
The proposal involves changing the use of the existing commercial building, which was previously received planning permission, to provide an Adult Day Services Hub.

According to the planning application, the proposed facility would include six facility rooms, toilet facilities and a passenger lift, along with minor changes to the building's elevations and internal modifications.
Permission is also being sought for an external garden activity space to the rear of the building, together with all associated site works.
The plans do not involve the construction of a new building, with the proposal instead involving the adaptation of the existing commercial premises for use as an adult day service.
Enable Ireland Disability Services is a registered charitable organisation providing services and supports to people with disabilities.
The application documentation states that the organisation has charitable status dating back to 1998, when it was known as Cerebral Palsy Ireland.

The company subsequently changed its name to the National Association for Cerebral Palsy (Ireland) Limited, before becoming Enable Holistic Services Ireland in 2000 and later Enable Ireland Disability Services.
The proposed hub would be located within the existing built-up area of Smithstown, with the application including plans for the internal layout, elevations, site layout and proposed garden area.
A number of documents have been submitted as part of the application, including a certificate of incorporation, landowner consent and architectural drawings.
A submission or observation in relation to the application can be made in writing to the planning authority for a prescribed fee of €20.
This must be done within five weeks of the authority first receiving the planning application.
The planning application was received by Clare County Council on July 14 and was validated on the same date.
Submissions or observations can be made to the planning authority until August 17, with a decision due on September 7.

title: Munster GAA Chair accused of putting Kerry before province when defeating Clare proposal & GAA top brass back continued Allianz sponsorship
excerpt: MUNSTER GAA Chairman Tim Murphy has come under fire for ‘putting Kerry before Munster’ when defeating a proposal from Clare GAA to take home advantage from Cork and Kerry in the Munster SFC semi-finals and finals.
author: Seamus Hayes
alt: Munster GAA Chair accused of putting Kerry before province when defeating Clare proposal & GAA top brass back continued Allianz sponsorship
body: MUNSTER GAA Chairman Tim Murphy has come under fire for ‘putting Kerry before Munster’ when defeating a proposal from Clare GAA to take home advantage from Cork and Kerry in the Munster SFC semi-finals and finals.

Clare GAA Chairman, Kieran Keating said it was a case of “GAA politics” when the matter was discussed at the August meeting of the County Board. At this meeting, Munster delegate Joe Garry said other options will now be explored by Clare.
The meeting was also informed that the most recent Central Council sitting had unanimous agreement that the GAA maintain its sponsorship with Allianz.

Informing this week’s Clare GAA board meeting of the Munster Council decision to vote against a proposal from Clare, Limerick, Waterford and Tipperary regarding the Munster senior football championship, Munster delegate Joe Garry said “we have other options”.

He outlined how delegates from the four counties voted in favour of having home advantage in championship games against Cork and Kerry while the current seeding arrangement remains in place. Cork and Kerry voted against the proposal as did the four officers of the Council, three of whom come from Waterford and Limerick. This tied the vote at 8-8 leaving the casting vote to the chairman who opposed the proposal from the four counties.
“In practical terms this is not how it works. We have other options. There will be another meeting before the Munster championship draw and this is something we have to look at”, Garry said.

Complimenting both Joe and his fellow Munster delegate John Callinan, board chairman Kieran Keating said “I know ye did very well in explaining the thinking behind the motion which we put. It’s unfortunate the any of the top table didn’t see reasons maybe to abstain and let the counties decide rather than voting on what the chairman wanted but I suppose that’s the nature of politics and the GAA. Sometimes you don’t know what deals have been agreed beforehand”.

“It’s frightening to see the selfishness of Kerry and Cork, there was no generosity. Joe gave stats that it wouldn’t really change anything in terms of results but it would make matters more competitive. We asked the chair to not just have the legacy of maintaining a Kerry – Cork Munster final but also to have a look at the Munster championship. I have been prevailed on in the short time that I have been there that I should be Munster, not Clare. It’s very disappointing”, Munster delegate John Callinan told the meeting.

According to Planning and training officer Paddy Smyth “this whole scenario is a bit off the wall. Four counties voted for the proposal with two against. There are only six counties in Munster. That’s not democracy. Four officers didn’t listen to the majority of the counties. What are we dealing with here. Their only goal should be to promote the GAA. We don’t want to talk to Kerry or Killarney UDC n whatever it is. We want to promote our games. That’s our brief and that should be their brief but it obviously isn’t”.

“It’s a disgrace really and as a Clare board we should let the Munster Council regularly know that we are very upset about the matter. They come to us lots of times looking for this that or the other”, Ambrose Heagney told the meeting.

Replying chairman Kieran Keating said “I know that the answer will be that it was voted on. The counties elected four officers, that’s who we have in place. It ended up 8-8 and the Chairman then had the casting vote. He is from Kerry and his plan is to have Cork/Kerry finals in Killarney and Cork so he wasn’t going to support our motion. We can’t protest that the vote wasn’t fair. We can have our debates with members of the executive who didn’t back us and who rowed in behind the chairman. That’s GAA politics, unfortunately”.

Ruan delegate Michael O’Regan said “It’s not great on behalf of the Chairman where they pay lip service in trying to promote the games in the so-called weaker counties and yet when there is an opportunity for the game to in played in some of the weaker counties that the big boys are afraid to travel outside their boundaries. It was wrong of the chairman to put himself in the position that he put Kerry before Munster, that is what it would be perceived as”.
The inter county masters fixtures plan for 2027 is “much the same as this year”, according to Central Council delegate Robert Frost who reported on a Central Council meeting held last week.
“The only thing, and it wouldn’t concern us is that they are talking about playing the Joe McDonagh cup final before an All-Ireland semi-final. There is for and against it. It’s yet to be decided”.

Continuing he told the delegates that “we had a long discussion about the Allianz sponsorship. It was unanimous that the GAA continue with the sponsorship as members couldn’t see any conflict of interest with what is happening in Gaza. It was pointed out that the GAA has made a major contribution through the Irish Red Cross in support of the people of Gaza”.

Clooney/Quin delegate John Skehan told the meeting that it was “an error to fix the Clooney/Quin vs Inagh/Kilnamona match in a direct clash with the All-Ireland football final (4p.m.). Something like a million people wanted to see and watched the All-Ireland football final. There were a lot of people at our match, players, mentors, officials gate checkers etc who wanted to watch the match. Under no circumstances should as tight a scheduling as that occur”.

According to Kieran Keating “that was an error. We would not have intended to have a clash like that. The All-Ireland final is a big day and generally, we try to keep that day as free as possible. With different grades, it can be difficult”.
Twenty Clare clubs have yet to nominate a demographic officer, delegates at this week’s county board meeting.

County demographic officer Neil O’Brien’s report was presented to the meeting by Kieran Keating who named the clubs Banner, Scariff, Tulla, Ballyvaughan, St Joseph’s Miltown, Michael Cusacks, Moy, Lissycasey, Liscannor, Kilkee/Bealaha, Shannon Gaels, Sixmilebridge, Coolmeen, Corofin, Kilmihil, Kilrush, Clonbony, Clondegad, Kilmurry Ibrckane, Cooraclare.

“Some of those are clubs that are quite big and some are quite small and challenged demographically. They all need to appoint a demographic officer as its quite hard for the county officer to work in a vacuum. He is trying to understand the data he is gathering in relation to who is in the different schools and what clubs they are attached to. He will be e-mailing those clubs”, the chairman said.

Replying to a query from Corofin delegate Fergal Neylon, Head of Operations Ann Marie Moran stated, “the demographic committee want information from each of the clubs maybe to do with numbers, registrations, ages etc”.

In his end of year report to Clare GAA, Celtic Challenge hurling manager Brian Culbert said they “held 70 training sessions including challenge games. They had 50 players from 23 different clubs and there was at least five championship matches for every player. There were eight top class coaches sharing their knowledge and a trophy to show for it and, most importantly, a whole lot of enjoyment, friendships and craic along the way”.

“We got to play all counties in Munster and Leinster. One team lost out to Tipperary in one semi-final and the second team went on to beat Waterford in the semi-final and Limerick in the final. Clare got more value in the Celtic challenge than any other county. Some counties get nothing for their players. Clare players are treated the way county players should be”, his report continued.
Clare GAA has applied to Croke Park for a grant from the infrastructure fund.

“We have applied for a grant to help with upgrading the toilets area at Cusack Park. In the past we have received aid from this fund for work at Cahsrlohan”, Kieran Keating told delegates at this week’s meeting.

title: Ballyea 'don't have full control' on their fate heading into final round
excerpt: BALLYEA “don’t have full control” on their future heading into the final round of the Clare SHC but they remain determined to deliver a performance that can keep their campaign alive.
author: Eoin Brennan
alt: Ballyea 'don't have full control' on their fate heading into final round
body: BALLYEA “don’t have full control” on their future heading into the final round of the Clare SHC but they remain determined to deliver a performance that can keep their campaign alive.

A first round defeat to Inagh/Kilnamona was followed by a second round draw with Clonlara that needs Ballyea requiring a win over St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield on Saturday evening while also hoping Inamona overcome Clonlara for them to advance to the last eight.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Ballyea boss Robbie Hogan outlined that they will endeavour to bring everything they can to the table in Newmarket-on-Fergus on Saturday (16:30). “We don’t have full control going into the final round but we still have something to play for. What we can control is our performance against Doora/Barefield so we’ll go wth the best possible attitude for that and hope others can do us a favour along the way too”.

Leading by two points with sixty six minutes played, Ballyea were left frustrated with the amount of additional time played by referee John Bugler as they let their lead slip to surrender a draw to Clonlara.

Five minutes of additional time were signalled by the referee but a row between both sides extended the allocated time, when play resumed Ian Galvin narrowed the gap to a point but while Mossy Gavin did well to defend a goalmouth scramble, he conceded a sideline cut which saw Micheál O’Loughlin find Aidan Moriarty who scored the equaliser.

Hogan was frustrated they didn’t hold on for the win. “When you’re a point up and there’s seven extra minutes played at the end, having been told five initially, we were obviously hoping to hang on but look a quality team like Clonlara were always going to right to the bitter end. Look we came in just looking for a performance and go back up the dual carriageway with lads having given everything and in fairness I could have asked for anymore from them from an effort point of view. Credit Clonlara too they made a great game of it and we knew it was going to be close because there are real quality players on both sides”.

Yet to record a win, the character is still clear to see within their side, Robbie maintained. “There’s great character in our lads and we managed to stay in front against the wind in the second half. We were actually playing up the hill and against the wind and thought we might snatch the two points but it just wasn’t to be. So we have to knuckle down again now quickly as there’s another game to be played and we’ll work out the permutations when we can recover from this one first”.

title: 63% of cigarette packs surveyed in Ennis had no Irish duty paid
excerpt: ALMOST two-thirds (63%) of cigarette packs surveyed in Ennis in 2026 were found to have no Irish duty paid, according to new research commissioned by JTI Ireland.
author: Paige Foley
alt: 63% of cigarette packs surveyed in Ennis had no Irish duty paid
body: ALMOST two-thirds (63%) of cigarette packs surveyed in Ennis in 2026 were found to have no Irish duty paid, according to new research commissioned by JTI Ireland.

The latest Empty Pack Survey, commissioned by JTI Ireland, found that 63% of packs surveyed in Ennis were non-Irish duty paid (NIDP), referring to tobacco products on which Irish tax has not been paid.
The category includes legal tobacco products purchased abroad as well as illegal products, including counterfeit cigarettes.

Of the packs surveyed in Ennis, 20% were identified as counterfeit cigarettes, the second-highest rate recorded among the 22 locations surveyed. Wexford had the highest rate at 25%, followed by Waterford at 19%.
Nationwide, 57% of packs surveyed were non-Irish duty paid, with counterfeit cigarettes accounting for 14%.
Galway recorded the highest rate of non-Irish duty paid cigarettes at 75%, followed by Swords at 66%.

Government figures cited by JTI indicate that the Irish Exchequer lost approximately €5 billion in tax revenue to non-Irish duty paid products since 2018, including around €1 billion in 2025 alone. JTI also cited Government figures showing €758 million was lost specifically to illegal tobacco products.

Daan van Hamersveld, Director of Corporate Affairs and Communications at Japan Tobacco International (JTI) Ireland, said the findings showed Ennis was among the areas of Ireland most affected by counterfeit cigarettes.
“These findings show that Ennis is one of the areas in Ireland hardest hit by illegal counterfeit cigarettes,” he said.

Mr van Hamersveld said illegal tobacco products were costing the State more than €750 million in lost taxes in 2025, while also undermining legitimate retailers and providing income for organised crime groups.

He said that, when legal non-Irish duty paid products were also included, retailers across the country were losing more than €1 billion in turnover annually as smokers turned to cheaper illegal and other non-Irish duty paid cigarettes.
He also claimed that the smoking rate has remained stable since 2019, suggesting smokers were seeking alternative channels in response to tax increases rather than quitting.
Mr van Hamersveld said JTI was calling on the Government to take a more moderate approach to excise increases while strengthening enforcement against cigarette smuggling and counterfeiting.

“We would urge the Government to pair a more moderate approach to excise increases with stronger enforcement action against the criminal networks behind cigarette smuggling and counterfeiting to avoid further exacerbating this already serious situation,” he said.

title: Safety concerns grow over 'lethal' speeding outside Coolmeen National School
excerpt: ROAD safety concerns have been raised outside Coolmeen National School, with councillors calling for a safety review amid complaints of speeding motorists approaching the village.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Safety concerns grow over 'lethal' speeding outside Coolmeen National School
body: ROAD safety concerns have been raised outside Coolmeen National School, with councillors calling for a safety review amid complaints of speeding motorists approaching the village.

The issue was raised by Cathaoirleach of the West Clare Municipal District, Cllr Michael Shannon (FF), who tabled a motion calling for a safety review of traffic at the junction of Hilltop Bar on the L2066 and the area surrounding Coolmeen National School, with particular attention to vehicle speeds on the bends approaching the school.

Cllr Shannon asked if the stretch of road could be included in the 2026 roads programme, saying the area “needs resurfacing”. He also called for a smaller programme of works to make the junction and the area outside the school safer, noting that the school is located on a bend.
He added: “As you go down to the Coolmeen church there is also a dangerous junction coming out there.”
Cllr Shannon highlighted that traffic approaching the village from the Kildysart side “come pretty fast”, as the road on that approach is “quite good”.
The motion was seconded by Cllr Dinny Gould (IND), who said he had received “a lot” of phone calls about speeding on the stretch of road, branding it “lethal”.
“Something has to be done to slow them down,” he said.

In a written response, Senior Executive Engineer Alan Kennelly said two road resurfacing projects had been completed in Coolmeen in recent years, adding that the improved road surface “may” have contributed to an increase in average vehicle speeds through the village.

Mr Kennelly noted that the enforcement of speed limits is a matter for An Garda Síochána and falls outside the remit of Clare County Council. He added that warning signs are already in place on both approaches to Coolmeen National School.
He said a Safe Routes to School scheme or a Low Cost Safety Scheme could help address road safety concerns and improve conditions for pedestrians and school users.

While the Municipal District intends to include Coolmeen National School in its application for Department of Transport funding this year, he stressed there is “no guarantee” the application will be successful.
Mr Kennelly added that the Municipal District would continue to engage with the elected member and explore future funding opportunities to deliver appropriate road safety improvements in the area.

title: Ennis housing estate marks 25 years of community
excerpt: Residents of Bruach na hAbhann on the Quin Road in Ennis have celebrated 25 years since the establishment of the community.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Ennis housing estate marks 25 years of community
body: Residents of Bruach na hAbhann on the Quin Road in Ennis have celebrated 25 years since the establishment of the community.
The anniversary celebrations took place on Saturday, 15th August, with many of the estate's original residents joining in the festivities.

Bruach na hAbhann was part completed by Luxury Homes (Galway) Ltd in July 2001, with the first residents moving into the estate that month. Twenty-five years later, many of those residents remain, as the estate has developed into a close-knit and active community.
To mark the anniversary, the Bruach na hAbhann Residents Association commissioned a new entrance stone, with support from Cllr Clare Colleran Molloy's Ennis Municipal District allocation.
The stone was designed and crafted by Michael McTigue and was formally unveiled during the celebrations.

Cllr Colleran Molloy (FF) congratulated residents on maintaining a strong sense of community over the past 25 years. Her support for the commemorative project, along with assistance from the team in Ennis Municipal District, was acknowledged by residents.
Davy Walsh, President of the Bruach na hAbhann Residents Association and a resident since the estate was established, paid tribute to successive residents' committees for their work over the years.
He said residents continued to take great pride in the upkeep of the estate and in maintaining the community spirit that had characterised Bruach na hAbhann since its earliest days.
The unveiling was followed by a Family Fun Day, with children's races, the Great Bruach Run, a penalty shoot-out and a Long Puc Challenge among the activities.
A highlight of the day was the presentation of medals by Munster Rugby scrum-half Ethan Coughlan, who grew up in Bruach na hAbhann.

Coughlan began his rugby career with Ennis Rugby Club before representing Ireland at underage level and captaining the Ireland U18s. He was also part of the Ireland U20 team that won the Six Nations Grand Slam in 2022 before progressing to senior rugby with Munster.
His achievements provided inspiration for the young people who took part in the sporting activities.
The celebrations concluded with a barbecue at neighbouring Johnno's Bar, where Donagh and his team provided food for more than 100 residents.
The Residents Association thanked the team at Johnno's for their generosity and for helping bring the celebrations to a fitting conclusion.

title: CLARE IFC: Banner & Cooraclare book quarter-final places, Naomh Eoin & Wolfe Tones bounce back & Clondegad keep cruising
excerpt: BACK TO BACK wins have secured qualification to the quarter-finals of the Clare intermediate football championship for Banner and Cooraclare.
author: Seamus Hayes
alt: CLARE IFC: Banner & Cooraclare book quarter-final places, Naomh Eoin & Wolfe Tones bounce back & Clondegad keep cruising
body: BACK TO BACK wins have secured qualification to the quarter-finals of the Clare intermediate football championship for Banner and Cooraclare.
With one round of games to go in the round robin stage of the TUS Clare IFC, only two of the twelve teams chasing honours, are assured of their places in the knock out stage.
Banner and Cooraclare with two wins from two outings are through while Clondegad who also have two wins from two outings are all but there.

Victory for Shannon Gaels over Clondegad and for Wolfe Tones over Liscannor in the final round would leave Clondegad, Wolfe Tones and Shannon Gaels each on four points and it would then be down to score difference to decide placings.
That said, Clondegad remain hot favourites not alone to qualify from the group but to be in the shake-up for honours.

Heading into the final round Liscannor, Coolmeen and Ennistymon remain bottom of their respective groups and each must win their final round games if they are to have a chance of avoiding the relegation play off.
Wolfe Tones 1-10 Shannon Gaels 0-6 Venue: Gurteen
Superior fitness and a great impact from their bench helped Wolfe Tones to a deserved victory over Shannon Gaels at Gurteen on Saturday evening.
A Shannon Gaels victory looked the likely outcome when they went to the break with a two point lead, 0-5 to 0-3 after playing against the wind.
They struck for the first point of the second half but that was to prove their only score in this period.

The winners had to wait until a minute before the end of the third quarter for their first score of the half which came from a Gary Leahy free. This score was followed by a disallowed goal from Wolfe Tones substitute Jack Ryan, referee Robert Harte penalising the Shannon man for picking the ball off the ground.

The game had just entered the final quarter when the winners introduced Eoghan Gough in attack in place of Gary Leahy and Gough quickly signalled his arrival with a brace of points, the first from a free, in the space of three minutes.
Then it was the turn of another substitute, Kevin Hanley, who pointed twice in the space of a minute and with five minutes remaining the Wolfe Tones men led on a score of 0-8 to 0-6.

Daithí Lohan extended his side’s lead to three points with four minutes of normal time remaining and with the final whistle fast approaching the winners struck for the game’s only goal. The Fitzgerald twins Tadhg and Niall, who had also been introduced in that final quarter, combined for Niall to apply the finish.
The game had just entered injury time when Eoghan Gough completed the scoring when converting a 20m free.
Tan Greene, Jayme O’Sullivan, Damien Lyne, Eoghan Casey and substitutes Eoghan Gough, Kevn Hanley and the Fitzgeralds made important contributions as Wolfe Tones got their first win in this campaign.
Goalkeeper Ciarán McCarthy made a number of good saves for Shannon Gaels while Aaron Lee McMahon, Eoin Keane, Jack Reidy, Thomas Kelly and Dylan Kenny got through some good work.

title: 'We can't turn a blind eye' – traffic calming sought outside Tulla GAA grounds
excerpt: TRAFFIC calming measures have been sought outside Tulla GAA amid ongoing concerns over speeding and pedestrian safety.
author: Paige Foley
alt: 'We can't turn a blind eye' – traffic calming sought outside Tulla GAA grounds
body: TRAFFIC calming measures have been sought outside Tulla GAA amid ongoing concerns over speeding and pedestrian safety.
While councillors said action was long overdue, Clare County Council warned that the rural location and 80km/h speed limit make the provision of a pedestrian crossing unlikely.

The issue was raised by Leas-Chathaoirleach of the Killaloe Municipal District, Cllr Conor Ryan (FG), who tabled a motion at the July meeting seeking traffic calming measures along the R352 adjacent to Tulla GAA grounds and improved pedestrian access to the town.
Cllr Ryan highlighted that this is an “ongoing issue” for the area due to “the speed of traffic flying by the road.”
He said he “understands the limits” given the GAA grounds are located along a regional road, but questioned what “hard or soft measures” could be implemented to reduce vehicle speeds.
Cllr Pat Hayes (FF) supported the motion, noting: “If you go back through the history books, we've all had motions down on this issue.”
“Just because we didn't sort it out back then, does not mean we haven't tried to find a solution,” he said, adding: “I don't think we can turn a blind eye.”

Referring to the “historic issue”, Cllr Hayes said events at the GAA grounds were not the main concern, but rather the day-to-day use of the road, saying: “It's one of those places where it's an issue to get kids to.”

In a written response, Senior Executive Engineer Declan Flanagan said Clare County Council had already delivered a number of active travel schemes in Tulla, including links to the athletics track and Tulla United FC, as well as a traffic calming scheme near St Mochulla’s National School.
However, he said those projects were located within the 50km/h speed limit zones and settlement boundary of Tulla, while the section of the R352 beside Tulla GAA presents additional challenges.
Mr Flanagan said the council had concerns regarding the provision of a pedestrian crossing at the location, particularly due to the road being a Strategic Regional Road with an 80km/h speed limit.

He said factors including traffic volumes, vehicle speeds, pedestrian numbers, road layout, crossing delays and safety records would all have to be considered when assessing whether crossing facilities could be provided.
“Primarily Zebra Crossings and Pelican crossings are installed in urban locations where speeds are low (50 to 60km/hr),” he said.

Mr Flanagan said the rural nature of the area, together with the alignment, width and volume of traffic on the R352, meant “it is unlikely that a speed reduction in this area to less than 80km/hr would be approved.”
He added that the issues raised in the motion could be examined as part of a future Local Transport Plan for Tulla, which is an objective under the Clare County Development Plan 2023-2029.

title: Clancy keen to give back to community that made him feel at home
excerpt: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s strong sense of community and pride of place can provide people with a vital sense of purpose and belonging, claims local psychotherapist and counsellor Fergal Clancy.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Clancy keen to give back to community that made him feel at home
body: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s strong sense of community and pride of place can provide people with a vital sense of purpose and belonging, claims local psychotherapist and counsellor Fergal Clancy.

Originally from Moycullen in Galway, Clancy has now lived in The Bridge for around seven years and has worked in counselling and psychotherapy for 15 years. After spending eight years working with the HSE drug and alcohol service, the self-confessed “blow-in” moved fully into private practice in 2025.

Now working three days a week from his home in Sixmilebridge, alongside two days in Galway and online sessions, Clancy says he has found the transition into private practice to be hugely rewarding. “It’s the best decision I ever made in my life really”, he explains.

“Working for organisations allowed me to bring my experience from the HSE to my private practice. When you’re working for yourself now, I’m literally my own boss. I can work my own hours, my own way with people”, Clancy continues.

“I’m very busy. They say it takes two to three years to develop a clientele, but I’m literally working all the time now really, to be honest”. Having recently begun greater promotion of his services both by word of mouth and online, the Moycullen man is hoping to become better known by the wider Sixmilebridge community. Specialising in men’s mental health and addiction counselling, Clancy highlights several particular challenges that can emerge in tightknit rural communities like Sixmilebridge.

“There’s a lot of farming in the area, so a lot of men, lone men, will go to the pub for a bit of social contact. It’s working with men in relation to that and men in breakups, separations, divorces. You’ve got to connect with the person. This is real life. This is what’s really going on for them”, he adds.

Using techniques such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), solution-focused therapy and motivational interviewing, the psychotherapist aims to focus on an individual's continual progression, saying “I don’t delve too much into the past unless it’s necessary. I say, is this the block to you moving forward?”.

That focus on moving forward also extends to his own relationship with Sixmilebridge, where Clancy says he has been made to feel at home since moving from his native Galway. The counsellor has been warmly welcomed by the people of The Bridge, noting that he “felt like I’ve moved from one home to another really. They’re very, very warm and welcoming. You’re a part of it straight away”.

Coming from a strong hurling background in Moycullen, Clancy understandably feels right at home in the heartland of Clare hurling, planning to get more involved with the 15 time Canon Hamilton winners in the near future.

The psychotherapist is also looking forward to becoming more involved in the Sixmilebridge Town Team, a local group backed by Clare County Council and Shannon MD responsible for the betterment of the community.

“I don't want to be just a person who comes and lives here and just works and that’s it. I want to get more involved in it and with the town plan and everything that's going forward, I'm excited for it and I'd love to be involved in it too. It would be something that I would get involved in because they've been so good to me. I want to give back to them too”, he adds.

title: Corofin on the cusp of knockout football while putting St Breckans on the brink of relegation battle
excerpt: COROFIN brought the fight and firepower to put themselves on the cusp of making the knockout stages of the Clare SFC while their North Clare derby win over St Breckans has the Spa on the brink of a relegation battle.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Corofin on the cusp of knockout football while putting St Breckans on the brink of relegation battle
body: COROFIN brought the fight and firepower to put themselves on the cusp of making the knockout stages of the Clare SFC while their North Clare derby win over St Breckans has the Spa on the brink of a relegation battle.
Corofin 1-13 St Breckans 0-9 Venue: Gurteen
Reigning intermediate champions Corofin have almost certainly consolidated their senior status for next season with their seven point win over St Breckans.

Seven points is a fair and accurate reflection on the gap between the sides in this outing. Corofin should they beat Kilmurry Ibrickane in round three will finish top of Group 3 and their scoring difference looks set to keep them from a relegation battle.

Two defeats from two has St Breckans slipping towards the relegation play-offs. Even a win against Lissycasey in the final round may not save them, such a scenario would put them equal on points with Lissycasey and potentially Corofin if they lose to the Bricks. Even then, the Spa’s scoring difference would require them to inflict a heavy beating on Cusack Cup champions Lissycasey.

From Seanán Kirby’s goal on fifteen minutes until the final whistle, Corofin were ahead apart from a quick Colm O’Brien equaliser. St Breckans took the lead twice in the opening quarter and held a 0-3 0-1 advantage before Kirby’s finish.
Both sides knew this was a game with the potential to define where their season heads but it was Corofin who showed far more desire.

An excellent Jamie Malone pass was finished soccer style to the net by Kirby for the game’s only goal on fifteen minutes. Moments previous, Tristan O’Callaghan had to be on alert to intercept a Kirby pass to Gearoid Cahill, clearing the resulting danger.

Sigerson Cup winner O’Callaghan got injured when attempting the same move on twenty minutes, a collision with Gearoid Cahill, saw him sustain a shoulder injury which ended his involvement in the game and prompted the introduction of Clare U20 panellist James Garrihy.

Cillian McGroary who was Corofin’s top scorer on the day, kicked a two pointer from a free in response to O’Brien’s equaliser. His attempt was made easier after the ball was moved forward for dissent by referee Barry Kelly after Donncha O’Dwyer made his views known to the match official. This indiscipline continued throughout the game, conceding eight frees in the second half when only winning three while O’Dwyer picked up a black card on fifty eight minutes.

McGroary’s two pointer was followed by scores from Gearoid Cahill and captain Kevin Keane to see Corofin hold a 1-5 0-4 interval lead. St Breckans were dealt a further blow when an ongoing injury is understood to have been behind the decision of captain Rowan Danaher getting called ashore before the break, even on occasions when he was getting bottled up or falling to the ground, Danaher made the right decision with his offloads so his presence was also missed.

There needed to a reignited St Breckans challenge on the restart but it never arrived, they conceded three points without reply, making it an unanswered burst of seven points either side of half time for Corofin. Jamie Stack finally opened their second half account on thirty nine minutes when converting a free, one which was awarded after Oisin Tierney took too long to take a kickout.
McGroary had the first two scores of the half for Corofin while Jamie Malone fisted over an effort to leave them seven in front on thirty seven minutes.

Excellent link-up play between Colm Breen, Gearoid Cahill and McGroary teed up Kirby for their ninth point on forty minutes while at the other end, Fionn Clancy made a great block on Cathal Morgan, the ball spilled to Jamie Stack who missed the target while a glorious goal chance was kept out when Oisin Tierney saved a one on one attempt by substitute Cathal Guerin, the resulting 45 was converted by Padraig Kelly.

Moments after entering the field of play, Cilléin Mullins managed to dislocate a finger which was swiftly put back into place and the Crusheen man had a hand to play in lining up Kirby for his second point of the day as Corofin fleshed out the lead to eight points.

An advanced mark from Stack and a two pointer from substitute Eoghan Garrihy were sandwiched between a Colm Breen white flag but the last score of the day would fall to Kevin Keane to seal the seven point win. Keane wouldn’t finish the game on the field, picking up a black card in additional time while Fionn Clancy was called upon again in defence, this time intercepting a Stack delivery to see them leave with a clean sheet.

Considering it finished 2-11 0-5 in St Breckans’ favour when the clubs last met in the Clare SFC, just two seasons ago, the nineteen point turnaround coupled with the derby aspect adds more sting to the loss. They’re all but confirmed for a relegation battle following successive defeats but as worrying as where they are headed is the performances.

Over the hour, they kicked fourteen wides, there was plenty of other mistakes but the indiscipline and lack of fight will be most concerning for the contingent from Doolin, Kilshanny and Lisdoonvarna. The big task facing Patrick O’Neill and his management is the lift a side short on morale and belief but they simply have to rise it because they are on a slippery slope. Cian Burke and Paddy Doherty did well to curb Jamie Malone and Gearoid Cahill to a point each but the lack of leadership and fight from within their ranks has to be addressed.

Celebrating not just a first SFC win since October 2022 when they beat Lissycasey by six points in the quarter-finals but more than likely regaining their status for next year, Corofin left Gurteen in high spirits and rightly so. They were stronger in the air with captain Kevin Keane central to them claiming aerial ball from restarts, they linked the play and moved the ball through the hands very well while other top performers included Colm Breen, Fionn Clancy, Cillian McGroary, Marc O’Loughlin and Seanán Kirby.
Peadar O’Brien’s side have a free shot at Kilmurry Ibrickane in two weeks and are showing glimpses of the side which reached the last four in 2022.

title: Dominance from Ennistymon's middle eight sees them advance to last eight & avenge Kilmihil loss
excerpt: ENNISTYMON’s senior footballers are en route to the Clare SFC quarter-finals after defeating Kilmihil by sixteen points, a big turnaround from their shock three point loss to the same opposition last season.
author: Eoin Brennan
alt: Dominance from Ennistymon's middle eight sees them advance to last eight & avenge Kilmihil loss
body: ENNISTYMON’s senior footballers are en route to the Clare SFC quarter-finals after defeating Kilmihil by sixteen points, a big turnaround from their shock three point loss to the same opposition last season.
Ennistymon 1-19 Kilmihil 0-06 Venue: Shanahan McNamara Memorial Park, Doonbeg

Definitely no upset this time around as Ennistymon’s growing maturity could be measured by a 19 point turnaround from last year’s result against the same opposition back in Shanahan McNamara Park in Doonbeg.

That sobering 0-16 to 0-13 defeat would have been central to their ruthlessness this time around as they led comfortably for the last 50 minutes to maintain their perfect start and cement a quarter-final spot with a game to spare.

What sums up the North Clare Magpies’ dominance most is that they raided for twenty scores through ten different players whereas Kilmihil could only muster up three, all from the boot of Martin O’Leary.

Ennistymon’s dominance stemmed from a powerful middle eight that ultimately sucked the life out of Kilmihil over the entire hour. With the wind at his back, Kilmihil talisman Martin O’Leary did provide the perfect start with a two point free after only 40 seconds but it would turn out to be an exception to the rule as Ennistymon may have taken eight minutes to repair their damage but once they did, there would only be one result.

Brendy Rouine was unlucky to see a goal chance deflected wide of the target but the county senior did convert three frees, two of which he won himself, while Josh Guyler, Mark Kelleher and Josh Vaughan ensured a 0-6 to 0-2 advantage by the midway mark off the opening half.

Again O’Leary punished with a two-point free entering the second quarter but it was quickly wiped out this time around as Darren McNamara (2), Brendy Rouine and Gearoid Barry provided the last four scores of the half to take a 0-10 to 0-04 advantage into the dressing rooms with the wind to come.

Any thoughts of a Kilmihil backlash or even another early O’Leary double soon evaporated on the resumption when a quick free picked out Eoin Rouine to beat the last defender and unleash a bullet to the roof of the Kilmihil net only four minutes into the new half.

Buoyed by that score, Ennistymon were hungry for more but a Josh Guyler back post effort hit the side-netting while Liam Cotter’s subsequent attempt cannoned off the left post but a brace of Sean Rouine points would allow the North Clare side brush off an O’Leary special entering the final quarter at 1-13 to 0-06.

Ennistymon emptied the bench and would be rewarded with the last seven points as substitutes Diarmuid Fahy (2) and Joe Concannon accentuated like scores for Brendy Rouine (2), Gearoid Barry and Eoin Rouine to ease up to a sixteen point triumph.

They may be in the last eight already but Declan Downes’ side will receive a stern preliminary quarter-final group decider against Kildysart in a fortnight’s time while his native club Kilmihil face an even more cut-throat winner-takes-all battle with St. Joseph’s Doora/Barefield that will see the winner advance to the knock-out stages and the loser spiralling into the demotion play-offs.

title: Process begins to have Kilbaha Pier road taken in charge by Clare County Council
excerpt: THE process to have the road leading from the R487 to Kilbaha Pier taken in charge by Clare County Council has begun after councillors backed the proposal at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Process begins to have Kilbaha Pier road taken in charge by Clare County Council
body: THE process to have the road leading from the R487 to Kilbaha Pier taken in charge by Clare County Council has begun after councillors backed the proposal at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District.

The motion was brought forward by Cllr Gabriel Keating (FG), who said the road is used by “many people”, including visitors who travel to nearby restaurants and may then wish to walk down to Kilbaha Pier.
He also highlighted that there is a private house located along the route and said taking the road in charge had been “on my agenda for quite a while”.
Cllr Keating thanked council officials for their response and welcomed their interest in the project, saying he was pleased that the process could now begin.
He said he would be relying on the support of his fellow councillors to progress the proposal and “get moving on the job”.
The motion was seconded by Cathaoirleach of the West Clare Municipal District, Cllr Michael Shannon (FF).

In a written response, Senior Executive Engineer Alan Kennelly said that, if adopted by members, the motion would initiate the statutory process under the Roads Act 1993 for taking a private road in charge.

Mr Kennelly outlined that the process would involve public consultation, consideration of any submissions received, preparation of an engineer's report, a further meeting of the municipal district and completion of post-consultation procedures before a final decision is made.

title: Tidy Towns seeks new generation of volunteers as Sixmilebridge grows
excerpt: RAPID growth in the size and population of Sixmilebridge has prompted a renewed push to attract younger residents and newcomers into the community, according to the PRO of the Sixmilebridge Community Development Association and Tidy Towns.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Tidy Towns seeks new generation of volunteers as Sixmilebridge grows
body: RAPID growth in the size and population of Sixmilebridge has prompted a renewed push to attract younger residents and newcomers into the community, according to the PRO of the Sixmilebridge Community Development Association and Tidy Towns.
Norma O’Neill became involved with the group almost by accident after contacting Sixmilebridge Tidy Towns about litter and dumping around forest entrances near her home.

“I had actually just been experiencing a lot of building at some forest entrances around the area. I’m a bit out of town in a townland called Cooleycasey and I would have made contact with the Tidy Towns first just to kind of hear about whether any grants were available or any place I could get pickers or bags. It was very innocent. It actually only started with a question about my own area outside the town and somehow I just got swept up in it”, the Sixmilebridge woman explains.

O’Neill outlines that the organisation has been in operation for more than 40 years and now faces the challenge of maintaining its strong volunteer base while attracting new members from a rapidly expanding population. Some of the group’s longest-serving members are now in their late seventies and approaching their eighties, making the recruitment of younger volunteers particularly important.

“I have noticed that some of the legends that are in the group, they're not getting any younger. You can't have people like that doing physical work. Whereas it’s quite a young population in the town. The population explosion that has happened in the last number of years is massive”.

With several new housing developments being constructed in and around the village, the group hopes to introduce itself directly to new residents and attract future members. “One of the aims we would have when the newest construction site on the Shannon Road is completed, we would be up to maybe three new developments where we want to get our campaign going. We want to drop leaflets and try to just introduce ourselves to people and get new members. We're always looking for new members”, O’Neill highlights.
In terms of weekly activities, the organisation has also introduced a regular volunteer work programme during the spring and summer months.

“We launched a volunteers work night which happens from March roughly to the end of September. We launch kind of a very intense work schedule where we have one or two nights every week for weeding, picking up litter, watering the flowers in the heat we had, that kind of thing”, O’Neill notes.

In recent years, the group has placed a greater emphasis on sustainability and encouraging a circular lifestyle within the community. One initiative involves working with local butcher Jamie Keane to provide a community sharing stand for surplus produce.

“It started with just an apple sharing program, but then we had people with cucumbers or tomatoes”, the PRO explains. The stand allows residents to leave excess fruit and vegetables for others to take, with the initiative expected to return in the coming weeks and continue through to September.

Sixmilebridge Community Development/Tidy Towns or SCDA also works with other community organisations in the village such as the GAA and Bridge United AFC. As The Bridge continues to grow, O’Neill hopes the next generation of residents will help shape the community as it moves forward. O’Neill’s message to anyone looking to become involved in the community is clear, “We’re always looking for new members, we’d be delighted to have you”, she adds.

Membership of Sixmilebridge Community Development/Tidy Towns or SCDA is free and open to anyone. Members will be added to a WhatsApp group after joining where they can hear about planned activities and volunteer. The group are on Instagram @sixmilebridgetidytowns and on Facebook @smbcommunitydevelopmen

title: Major aircraft maintenance facility proposed for Shannon Airport
excerpt: A MAJOR new aircraft Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facility has been proposed for Shannon Airport, with plans lodged for a new hangar building, staff accommodation and associated infrastructure.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Major aircraft maintenance facility proposed for Shannon Airport
body: A MAJOR new aircraft Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) facility has been proposed for Shannon Airport, with plans lodged for a new hangar building, staff accommodation and associated infrastructure.
Wonderlight Ltd has submitted a planning application to Clare County Council for the development at Lindbergh Avenue and Earhart Avenue, Shannon Airport.

The development would include the construction of a two-storey building, with the ground floor providing a four-bay aircraft hangar alongside training facilities, storage areas, toilets, plant rooms and other ancillary spaces.
The first floor would include staff accommodation, offices, a canteen, conference rooms and locker facilities, while the building would also feature rooftop solar panels and corporate signage.

The planning statement submitted with the application says the facility would support the continued growth of operations at Shannon Airport and allow for the expansion of aircraft maintenance services and employment in the region.

The plans include a new vehicle and pedestrian access from Lindbergh Avenue, improved pedestrian links to the existing bus stop on Airport Avenue, internal circulation areas and four taxi apron zones connecting to the existing aircraft taxiway.
A new surface car park with 199 spaces is proposed, including accessible parking and electric vehicle charging spaces, along with sheltered bicycle parking for 23 bicycles.

The development would also include a chemical and refuse storage building, an ESB substation/switchroom, two generator structures, a gas skid installation, underground static storage water tanks and a foul pumping station connection to the existing sewer network.
The application also includes the removal of an existing outbuilding, tanks, concrete yard and associated hardstanding areas at the site.
During site investigations, contaminated soil, including PFAS-impacted material linked to the site’s former use as a fire training ground, was identified.
The planning documents state that this material would be excavated and relocated to a designated containment berm within the site.

The proposed development is located on lands zoned for “Airport” development under the Shannon Town and Environs Local Area Plan, with the applicant stating that the MRO facility is compatible with the airport zoning objective.

A Natura Impact Statement accompanied the application because of the site's proximity to the Lower River Shannon Special Area of Conservation and the River Shannon and River Fergus Estuaries Special Protection Area.
A submission or observation in relation to the application can be made in writing to the planning authority for a prescribed fee of €20.
This must be done within five weeks of the authority first receiving the planning application.
The application was lodged on July 31, 2026, with submissions accepted until September 3. Clare County Council is due to make a decision by September 24.

title: Corofin look to catch fire at St Breckans' expense
excerpt: COROFIN maintain a second round Clare SFC win over St Breckans at “worst case” will result in a preliminary quarter-final place.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Corofin look to catch fire at St Breckans' expense
body: COROFIN maintain a second round Clare SFC win over St Breckans at “worst case” will result in a preliminary quarter-final place.

Both Corofin and St Breckans lost out in round one to Lissycasey and Kilmurry Ibrickane in round one of Group 3. The North Clare sides are eyeing up victories this weekend to put themselves back in the reckoning for getting out of the group rather than sweating until the final round to try pick up points.
Whoever prevails this weekend will be level on points with the loser of the Lissycasey and Kilmurry Ibrickane tie, provided it doesn’t end in a draw.

Ahead of Sunday’s showdown in Gurteen (15:00), Corofin manager Peadar O’Brien stated, “Whoever wins that game is going in the worst case get to a preliminary quarter-final but there is a lot of football to be played still. St Breckans are quite capable of beating Lissycasey, Kilmurry Ibrickane won’t want to let anyone beat them so you don’t know how it will go, you could finish up with three teams on two points or three teams on four points, there is a lot to play for”.

Having fell 1-8 0-0 behind in the opening half, Corofin took twenty nine minutes to get off the mark in their return to the Clare SFC. “We found it difficult to get to the pace in the first half, we couldn’t live with them, we couldn’t get a hand on them, the two pointers are a major game-changer, we went from eight down to only three minutes later being within two points, we found it difficult and the couple of injuries didn’t help us but everyone has them. We found it difficult to get to the pace of the game in the first half particularly”.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, O’Brien acknowledged their slow start was to do with the jump from intermediate to senior and lining out in the Garry Cup. “There is a bit of that in it definitely, there is a bit of a difference playing Cusack Cup versus Garry Cup, I know it is not taken majorly serious in either case but at the same time there is a difference in pace and you can see the quality Lissycasey have especially with their forward players, they are really good footballers, technically they are good footballers and good scorers, they have four or five forwards capable of scoring on any given day. We were putting fires out all over the place, it wasn’t that anyone was doing serious damage but they were all doing a bit of damage, it all adds up”.

Trailing by thirteen points with thirty nine minutes on the clock, Corofin kicked into gear scoring 1-8 without reply, a run that could well prove vital if scoring difference comes into play after the final round. “If we’re truthful the first half was embarrassing, at least we showed a bit and we were there at the end, with five minutes to go they were starting to sweat because we had all the momentum and a bit of a head of steam up, we were starting to motor which is all we can ask for, we want to be in the game towards the end of it and hopefully we’ll be in that position for the next two rounds and hopefully get something out of one of them, that should be enough,” Peadar commented.

Damien O’Loughlin and Cilléin Mullins were both missed from their defence in round one, O’Brien is hopeful they may feature this weekend. “We’d be hoping Damien would definitely be back, we’re not sure about Cilléin”.

title: Éire Óg come up trumps after stiff test from Doonbeg
excerpt: CHAMPIONS Éire Óg survived a stern test from Doonbeg as they came moments from suffering their first championship defeat in the county in normal time in five years.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Éire Óg come up trumps after stiff test from Doonbeg
body: CHAMPIONS Éire Óg survived a stern test from Doonbeg as they came moments from suffering their first championship defeat in the county in normal time in five years.
Éire Óg 2-15 Doonbeg 3-9 Venue: Páirc na Muintire, Lissycasey
A three point final margin doesn’t even come close to underlining how narrow the gap was between Éire Óg and Doonbeg in round two of the Clare SFC.

It’s the first time since their 2020 quarter-final exit to Kilmurry Ibrickane in Cooraclare that Éire Óg have conceded three goals in the Clare SFC but crucially for them, they came out on the winning side this time round and it puts them through to the quarter-finals for the tenth year in a row.

Noted for their talent and ability to score from all angles, this was an Éire Óg showing where their workrate, appetite and tackling came to the fore. Oran Cahill, Ikem Ugwueru and Darren O’Brien setting the standard in this regard. The hunger shown by the Townies to stem the tide and win back possession helping them to avoid a first championship loss since the 2023 semi-finals where they bowed out on a penalty shootout.

Doonbeg deserved something from this game but ended up with nothing. The morale victory will be of no consolation as they have no points from two games and it will all come down to their final round showdown with Cratloe where the winner advances to the quarter-finals and the loser ends up in the relegation series.

Three goals were put past the Townies but they responded strongly to the second and third major. They came back with a bang to Doonbeg’s third green flag, kicking six points in succession which was ultimately the period where they claimed victory and the Magpies fell to defeat.

Level three times inside the first half, Doonbeg playing with the aid of a slight breeze only trailed once in the opening half. They only went ahead once in the second half, following Killeen’s forty ninth minute major but only added another point from here to the final whistle as Éire Óg packed a punch at the defining moment of the tie.

Adding an ironic twist to the tale was Mark McInerney once again emerging as Éire Óg’s leading scorer. That McInerney was the scorer in chief for the Ennis side is no surprise but this was against the club of his father, Doonbeg icon Francis McInerney a winner of seven senior titles with the Magpies.

Mark was first on the board with a pointed free on four minutes before Doonbeg landed a brace of two pointers, Seán Conway making his first championship start since 2024 and one of this year’s breakthrough players Darragh O’Sullivan on target within 111 seconds of each other.

Down the left flank, Darren O’Brien caused probems, he kicked two points in a row, the first made by Ikem Ugwueru and the second from McInerney but O’Brien certainly had his shooting boots with him in Lissycasey. McInerney levelled matters for the first time on ten minutes, kicking off his left boot before Eoin Killeen jinked past Dean Ryan to restore Doonbeg’s one point lead.
Ronan Lanigan powered forward to get Éire Óg back on level terms, Gavin Murray, Darren Moroney and Ugwueru all involved in the build-up as McInerney finished off the move on twelve minutes.

Gavin O’Shea and Ugwueru swapped scores before Doonbeg hit for two goals in three minutes. A shot from Darragh O’Sullivan appeared to be drifting wide but Eoin Killeen was on alert and palmed it to the net while it was Killeen who was fouled leading to Chris Maguire awarding a penalty which Mikie Tubridy calmly slotted beyond Bernard Power to put Brian Shanahan’s side 2-06 0-6 in front on twenty four minutes.

Swift responses would prove to be Éire Óg’s forte and they struck for goal in their next attack. Tadhg Lillis did tremendously to block a certain McInerney point but the ball broke into the square where David Loftus recycled back to Luke Pyne and he finished superbly to the bottom right corner of Éamonn Tubridy’s net. McInerney was on target with his next effort, a free which narrowed the gap to two points for half-time.

Scores were drying up on the restart, it took eight minutes for the first contribution to the scoreboard of the second half but it was a significant one. Mark McInerney pounced for goal after Éire Óg overturned a Doonbeg kickout, Darren Moroney doing well and the Clare vice captain made no mistake when the opportunity to goal came his direction.

Over the next eleven minutes, Doonbeg got level twice, Darragh Burns and David Tubridy equalising while Ikem Uguweru picked off his second point of round two and Jack Joyce marked his arrival with a score. Tubridy introduced as a substitute, scored a free with his first touch but the former Clare stalwart was also alert to claim a break in the middle third.
There was a tremendous block from Ronan Lanigan to prevent Mikie Tubridy raising another green flag.

It was Tadhg Lillis that won the turnover which led to Doonbeg’s third goal, Lillis drove forward after winning the ball back and the lively Eoin Killeen again proved too hot to handle for the Éire Óg defence as he nicked in for their third goal and his second on forty nine minutes.

As the game now entered the final ten, Éire Óg knew they had to up the ante, Jack Joyce had an effort cleared from danger by Jason Linnane while a bullet from McInerney was denied by the post. At the other end, Manus Doherty and Aaron Fitzgerald had to do a double act to block Darragh Burns.

Scores were needed and they came via McInerney with three, a two pointer from Darren O’Brien and Danny Lyne showed maturity to fist over in additional time. Eoin Killeen added another point for Doonbeg while they had a chance from a free which would have been a two pointer to reduce the gap to one but Eamonn Tubridy’s effort drifted to the left of the goal.

Having got a scare but still prevailed, this is a timely jolt for Shane Daniels’ Éire Óg. The champions received no test from Cratloe in round one but they were pushed all the way by Doonbeg and they came up with the goods. David McNamara’s physicality was a loss in the middle third but Oran Cahill and Darren O’Brien really stepped up with their workrate and leadership. Mark McInerney, Ikem Ugwueru and Ronan Lanigan also impressed for the Townies.

Another defeat would leave Doonbeg in a relegation battle but they don’t deserve to be in such a predicament having performed well in both of their championship outings. Howeve results will dictate their future and they need to prevail over Cratloe to avoid fighting for their status and instead showing what they can do in the business end. Standout performers for Doonbeg were Tadhg Lillis, Eoin Killeen and Seán Conway.

title: Cratloe left in a Hayes after goalkeeper inspires Miltown
excerpt: Goals wins games but so do goalkeepers as Cóilin Hayes proved more difficult than the Strait of Hormuz to pass for St Joseph’s Miltown to maintain their perfect start to the Clare SFC as Cratloe fell to a second loss.
author: Eoin Brennan
alt: Cratloe left in a Hayes after goalkeeper inspires Miltown
body: Goals wins games but so do goalkeepers as Cóilin Hayes proved more difficult than the Strait of Hormuz to pass for St Joseph’s Miltown to maintain their perfect start to the Clare SFC as Cratloe fell to a second loss.
St Joseph’s Miltown 3-13 Cratloe 0-20 Venue: Páirc Finne, Corofin

The ultimate difference between the sides was that Miltown were simply more clinical in front of the posts as twice Darragh McDonagh used his strength to hold off his marker and fire to the net to add to a first half major for Euan Lineen while down the other end, the West Clare side relievedly survived eight goal scares.

Teenager Hayes prevented five of them including a first half trio of impressive stops from Jamie Moylan while remarkably Hayes got even better as the game developed, repelling a Diarmuid Ryan bullet before capping off an exemplary man-of-the-match display by tipping away a Podge Collins 55th minute penalty.
Had Cratloe scored, it would have regained full parity but instead an inspired Miltown held on for a second successive group win.

With both side craving victory, it was arguably the game of the championship to date in terms of speed, intensity and end-to-end action aided by Fergal O’Brien’s free-flowing refereeing style. The copious amount of timely goal chances also added to the entertainment value that produced four sightings alone in the first six minutes.

With the wind at their backs, a much more driven Cratloe were settled by a Ryan Harkin two-pointer after only 40 seconds but from the kick-out, Rian Considine and Sean Collins combined to play in Jamie Moylan whose shot was parried by goalkeeper Hayes.

Targetman Moylan’s power and pace were a heady cocktail for Miltown to contend with but Paul Frawley intercepted a pass from him close to goal before Cóilin Hayes excellently tipped away another Moylan attempt by the fourth minute.
Cratloe goalkeeper Cian O’Gorman was just as effective as he kept out a Euan Lineen shot while also arrowing over a ’45 to boost his side to a 0-4 to 0-1 lead.
Darragh McDonagh set up Micheál Murray and Eoin Cleary for points to reel in Cratloe while a defiant rearguard blocked successive efforts through Conor Ryan and a frustrated Moylan.

Diarmuid Ryan did convert a two-pointer by the midway mark of the half, only to be floored from the restart as Paul Frawley, Cian Mahony, Oisin Looney and Frawley again combined to set up Euan Lineen for a cool low finish to the bottom right corner of the Cratloe net.

Eoin Cleary tagged on a brace of points to hand Sean O’Brien’s side a 1-6 to 0-6 cushion and it was needed as Cratloe’s best forward Ryan Harkin responded with two points of his own. Cóilin Hayes saved his best stop for a point-blank Jamie Moylan piledriver while Euan Lineen just cleared the crossbar to see Miltown inch into the dressing rooms 1-08 to 0-10 in front.
That pattern would be maintained on the resumption as now backed by the conditions, Miltown did their best to shake off their obstinate opponents but with little success.

An Eoin Cleary two-pointer was bolstered by another Hayes save, this time from Diarmuid Ryan but the ball would be in the opposite net only seconds later when Paul Frawley’s delivery was caught and powered to the net by Darragh McDonagh at 2-10 to 0-12 by the 36th minute.

The returning Podge Collins stepped up with two goal chances that both must went the wrong side of the crossbar but they did bookend a four point unanswered blitz to level the tie for only a fourth time by the two-thirds mark at 2-10 to 0-16.

That would be the last time that the sides would be locked together though as an almost identical second Darragh McDonagh goal at the turn of the final quarter provided the cushion for Miltown to cling to albeit that it had to take a full length stop from the cat-like Hayes to prevent Podge Collins from equalising after a foul on substitute Cathal Lohan.

That intervention effectively cemented St. Joseph’s Miltown’s place in the last eight and a further barometer in a group decider against a three-in-a-row chasing Éire Óg while for 2023 champions Cratloe, it’s now winner-takes-all in their final round showdown against Doonbeg to see who advances to the business end and which side ends up in the sharp end.
