title: Doora/Barefield & Kildysart ends in a draw for second year in a row
excerpt: FOR THE second year in a row, St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield and Kildysart have finished all square in the Clare SFC.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Doora/Barefield & Kildysart ends in a draw for second year in a row
body: FOR THE second year in a row, St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield and Kildysart have finished all square in the Clare SFC.
St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield 3-12 Kildysart 3-12 Venue: Clarecastle
Though they were level just three times over the hour, as ever there was very little between Kildysart and St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield who met in the Clare SFC for the third year running.
Clarecastle has been the setting for their close encounters over the last three seasons, the one point win in 2024 for Kildysart the only instance of the three when it hasn’t ended in a draw.

Leading by five points with five minutes of normal time remaining, Doora/Barefield were well on their way to bouncing back into the Jack Daly race following their disappointing opening round loss to Ennistymon.
Instead, they conceded two goals in ninety seconds and ended up fortunate to rescue a draw with Tom McDonald equalising from a tricky angle in the last attack of the afternoon.

Michael Nash’s return from Chicago was a big lift for the Doora/Barefield. He only returned from the Windy City to the Parish on Friday evening but made his presence known immediately in Clarecastle when kicking the opening two scores of the game.

In only his second competitive club start since suffering an ACL injury last July, Emmet McMahon began to show glimpses of his top form and fired eight points over the hour, finishing as their leading scorer.

Nash’s scores followed by a Tom Curran effort, made by Cian McDonough helped Doora/Barefield into a 0-3 0-1 lead by the third minute, Kieran O’Brien fisting over Kildysart’s score after Conor Moloney timed his run to capture a break from a Conor Cusack kickout.

Kuba Ruminowicz pulled off his first big save of the day to deny Diarmuid O’Donnell a goal for Kildysart on seven minutes but in their next effort, they kicked a two pointer when Luke McGrath was fouled and McMahon made no mistake with the resulting free, levelling matters on ten minutes.

McMahon and Tom McDonald traded scores before Eoin Lahiffe opened his account, scoring his first goal in championship football after palming an Eoghan Thynne delivery to the net on fifteen minutes, the move stemming from a Killian McIlroy turnover which was then made by Tom McDonald and Odhran O’Connell covering the ground.
Thynne was on hand to set up Lahiffe again moments later, this time the dual player split the posts to have Doora/Barefield four clear.

Then came Kildysart’s biggest scoring spree of the day, they hit 1-3 without reply in six minutes, McMahon, Liam Casey and Luke McGrath converting points with Diarmuid O’Donnell controlling a long-range delivery and firing to the net to give them a two point advantage with twenty four minutes played. There would be no more Kildysart scores for the remainder of the half while Joe Rafferty reduced it back to a on point game with a well-taken point.
Jamie Evans marked his introduction at the interval by setting up Emmet McMahon for the half’s first score, seventy seconds in to restore the two point advantage for Kildysart.

Doora/Barefield missed their first four shots of the second half but Odhran O’Connell steadied the ship with his first championship point on thirty five minutes, the younger brother of Carlton Blues’ Siofra Ní Chonaill was noted for stepping up with valuable goals last season. Liam Casey responded in Kildysart’s attack and it was back to a two point game.

Stepping up with his first championship score in the maroon and white of Doora/Barefield was John Sheanon who finished an excellent team move to the back of the net. The two-time All-Ireland club winner with Cuala made his debut when introduced from the bench and was in the right place at the right time after Joe Rafferty and Eoin Lahiffe linked the play impressively to tee him up.
Lahiffe picked off his second point of the day when once again Eoghan Thynne was the provider, the Avenue Utd midfielder made an excellent turnover when forcing the Kildysart defence under pressure.
Heading into the final quarter, the teams were tied when Emmet McMahon kicked a two pointer from a free but another big push from Doora/Barefield was to follow.

They capitalised on an overcooked Liam Casey pass to McMahon with Michael Nash bombing forward to fire over his third point. Then came their third goal when Joe Rafferty pounced as Fergal Ginnane spilled a dropping ball out of his hands, took on Cillian Kelly and struck to the bottom left corner of the net. McDonald then set up Lahiffe and Doora/Barefield’s blitz of 1-2 in three minutes had them five clear with eight minutes remaining.
McMahon and Rafferty swapped scores to leave the margin of five with fifty six minutes on the clock but there was to be more twists and turns yet.

Keith O’Connor palmed to the net on fifty nine minutes to make it a two point game, a Luke McGrath delivery kept in by Diarmuid O’Donnell who fired the ball across goal, Doora/Barefield arguing that O’Connor was in the square at the time.

Doora/Barefield gifted possession to Kildysart on the kickout, Kuba Ruminowicz should have gone long with his delivery but some of his main targets tried to make themselves options up short, it caught them with O’Connor winning the ball before Sheanon, he popped to Oisin Coyle who had quick hands to offload to Jamie Evans but Kuba kept his shot out but was unable to stop Jack Cotter’s rebound and with the game in additional time Kildysart were ahead by one.
From a very tight angle, Tom McDonald equalised in a patient next attack from Doora/Barefield leaving both sides settling for a share of the spoils.

Both sides have cases to make that it was a point loss from their various perspectives. Doora/Barefield dominated the second half and had themselves home and hosed, leading by five with four minutes of normal time remaining, they switched off defensively and conceded two soft goals, having played the better football in the second half,

Meanwhile, Kildysart had been the stronger side in the opening half and with Emmet McMahon on form they were keeping their noses in front. They’ll be fuming at having put themselves in a position to snatch the victory that they let it slip through their fingers.

title: 'The speed of cars is frightful' – Footpath campaign faces major obstacles in West Clare
excerpt: A PETITION from residents of a West Clare community calling for a footpath and traffic calming measures has renewed concerns over speeding on the approach to Kilrush.
author: Paige Foley
alt: 'The speed of cars is frightful' – Footpath campaign faces major obstacles in West Clare
body: A PETITION from residents of a West Clare community calling for a footpath and traffic calming measures has renewed concerns over speeding on the approach to Kilrush.

The issue was raised by Cllr Dinny Gould (IND) at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District, where he called for a review of speeding and traffic calming measures at Leadmore, as well as the exploration of a footpath with public lighting linking the area to Kilrush. He also highlighted a petition signed by local residents seeking action.
He said the proposal had previously been brought forward by Independent Cllr Ian Lynch, but little progress had been made.

He described speeding in the area as “dangerous”, particularly during the summer months as traffic increases between Kilrush and Kilkee, and said residents could not understand why the long-sought project had yet to be delivered.
“The speed of cars is frightful,” he told the meeting.

Seconding the motion, Cllr Gabriel Keating (FG) said efforts had been made before the Covid-19 pandemic to advance the project, but said requirements set by Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) had proved a major obstacle.
“The speeds cars are going is unbelievable,” he said.
Cllr Ian Lynch (IND) said residents needed to understand the challenges involved.
“We need to explain the challenges to people and that we are not ignoring them,” he said, adding that some of the issues were outside the council's control.

In a written response, Senior Executive Engineer Alan Kennelly said the proposed footpath would be located almost entirely along a section of the N67 subject to a 100 km/h speed limit, meaning approval from Transport Infrastructure Ireland would be required before the project could proceed.
He said the proposal was likely to be inconsistent with national planning policy for National Secondary Roads and, as a result, it was considered unlikely that TII approval would be forthcoming.
Mr Kennelly also cited engineering challenges including the narrow road width, peat embankments and nearby property boundaries, which would make construction difficult and expensive.
He said construction costs alone were likely to exceed six figures, with additional expenditure required for land acquisition, accommodation works and major earthworks.

While Clare County Council has no current plans to advance the project, Mr Kennelly said the Municipal District would continue to engage with the elected member and explore future funding opportunities. He added that an appropriate funding source would need to be identified before a project of this scale could proceed.
Responding at the meeting, Mr Kennelly said he had met local residents and explained the issues involved, describing the proposal as one that had been under discussion “for a while”.
“If we got the blessing from TII we could pursue funding, but at the minute it would be in breach of national road guidelines policy,” he said.
Cathaoirleach of the West Clare Municipal District, Cllr Michael Shannon (FF), highlighted: “It is important to note that the houses were there before TII was formed.”

title: Community support helps Hazel turn salon dream into reality
excerpt: SIXMILEBRIDGE is a community to be proud of, says Hazel O’Callaghan, owner of KV Hair by Hazel.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Community support helps Hazel turn salon dream into reality
body: SIXMILEBRIDGE is a community to be proud of, says Hazel O’Callaghan, owner of KV Hair by Hazel.

Originally from Ennis, O’Callaghan says that establishing her own business in 2023 was one of the biggest milestones of her career but she could not have anticipated the level of support she would receive from the Sixmilebridge community.

“The support that I've got from the local community has been quite overwhelming and I'm very grateful for it. I’ve been supported from dot since moving here for which I’m very lucky That support has meant more to me than words can express. The trust people have placed in me, the friendships I've built, and the loyalty of my clients have all played a huge part in the success of my business”, the owner highlights.

After qualifying in her profession, O’Callaghan moved to Australia after being sponsored to work there, spending four and a half years managing a hair salon and barber shop, gaining invaluable experience and developing my skills in both hairdressing and barbering. That experience translated well into her Sixmilebridge enterprise in 2023 as the Ennis woman provides a welcoming space where everyone feels comfortable, valued, and leaves looking and feeling their very best.

“To come home years later and be able to bring all of that experience into my very own salon is something I’m incredibly proud of. It’s not just a business to me it’s something I’ve built around my career, my family and my passion for what I do”, O’Callaghan notes.

The owner says that the most enjoyable aspects of the job are the different conservations she has with each client as days can include everything from classic men’s haircuts and the latest skin fades and bobs to long layered trims, colours, highlights, curly blow-dries and up styles.

Family is to the core of KV Hair by Hazel, even giving the business its name as O’Callaghan explains that “The K represents my son, Koda, and the V represents my daughter, Vogue. Running a business while being a mother can certainly be challenging, but being a mum is the most important role I will ever have. Everything I’m building is not only something I’m passionate about, but something I hope my children can be proud of too”, she adds.

The hairdresser reiterates her gratitude to the customers and members of the community who have supported her since opening, saying “I want to thank every person who has walked through my door, recommended my business, or simply stopped for a chat. Your support has helped turn a dream into a reality and I’ll always be grateful for that”.

title: Ennistymon public toilets could reopen after vandalism forced closure
excerpt: THE reopening of Ennistymon's public toilets has been sought, with councillors arguing the facilities are essential for a town that is “extremely busy” year-round.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Ennistymon public toilets could reopen after vandalism forced closure
body: THE reopening of Ennistymon's public toilets has been sought, with councillors arguing the facilities are essential for a town that is “extremely busy” year-round.

The issue was raised by Cllr Shane Talty (FF) at the July meeting of the West Clare Municipal District, where he called for immediate measures to reopen the public toilets, arguing that the recent investment in the facilities “cannot just be abandoned”.
Cllr Talty said the current situation was “not good enough”, pointing to Ennistymon's “success story” in terms of the number of businesses that remain open in the town.
The motion was seconded by Cllr Bill Slattery (FG), who said the facilities had been sought by the community for between 15 and 20 years before finally opening.
He noted that the toilets were well used, particularly by people walking near the Falls Hotel, and described their closure as “a huge loss to the town”.

Director of Service Carmel Kirby said she would “equally support” efforts to reopen the toilets but stressed that the council first needed to find a way to overcome the anti-social behaviour that had led to their closure.
She suggested measures to manage access to the facilities could be explored, including the possibility of making a key available through the local library for people to request use of the toilets.
Cathaoirleach for the district, Cllr Michael Shannon (FF), also backed the proposal, saying the availability of public toilets was especially important given the influx of tourists to Clare.
“We want to present the best foot we can and these are the minimum requirements we need to have for our tourists coming into the west of Ireland,” he said.
Cllr Joe Killeen (FF) also formally supported the motion.

In a written response, Acting Senior Engineer Paddy Tiernan said councillors would be aware that the public toilets were reopened in 2024 following a significant investment by Clare County Council, including refurbishment works and the installation of an external lift to improve accessibility.
However, he said the facilities, including the lift infrastructure, were subjected to repeated vandalism and anti-social behaviour in the months after reopening, ultimately forcing their closure.

Mr Tiernan said the Municipal District was “not opposed in principle” to reopening the toilets, but any decision would have to be accompanied by measures to prevent further vandalism and ensure the long-term sustainability of the facility.
He said reopening the toilets would require a further significant investment to repair the damage, alongside appropriate maintenance and management arrangements.

While no funding has currently been identified, the Municipal District will examine the extent of the repairs required and the associated costs to help determine whether the facilities can be reopened and what funding options may be available.

title: Derby duels on the double for Downes & Denis in Ennistymon vs Kilmihil rematch
excerpt: ENNISTYMON head into the second round of the Clare SFC against Kilmihil “with our eyes wide open” in what is a derby duel on the double.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Derby duels on the double for Downes & Denis in Ennistymon vs Kilmihil rematch
body: ENNISTYMON head into the second round of the Clare SFC against Kilmihil “with our eyes wide open” in what is a derby duel on the double.

For the second year on the bounce, round two pits Ennistymon and Kilmihil. Last year, a Dan Keating inspired Kilmihil caused one of the shocks of the Clare SHC when overturning their North Clare opponents 0-16 0-13.

It’s back to Shanahan McNamara Memorial Park in Doonbeg when the sides renew their rivalry, Ennistymon will be determined not to make the same mistakes while Kilmihil need to win to reignite their championship following a first round loss to Kildysart.

On either sideline will be coaches facing off against their native clubs. Declan Downes is in his second season as Ennistymon manager, he represented Kilmihil at all levels and was part of their 2008 team to win the Clare intermediate football championship, he was one of their leading scorers in that campaign and the Downes name is synonymous with Kilmihil and not just football in the parish.

Former FAI CDO, Denis Hynes a proud Ennistymon man is coach of the Kilmihil senior footballers this season. It’s not his first time involved in the Clare SFC, he was coach to the Noel Crowe managed Ennistymon senior footballers who emeged from a tricky Group 1 in 2021 where they defeated Cratloe and Cooraclare, lost to Kilmurry Ibrickane and St Joseph’s Miltown before exiting to Éire Óg in the quarter-finals which saw the Townies reach the semi-finals for the first time since 2014 before claiming the Jack Daly.

Speaking to The Clare Echo, Downes said the lessons from last year’s loss to Kilmihil must be put into practice. “We’re going in with our eyes wide open, I didn’t see the game versus Kildysart but I’ve plenty of people telling me they gave a really good account of themselves, they will fight tooth and nail, they are a proud bunch and I know them well, I’ve no doubt of what is coming ahead of me and these guys have as well, there is a lesson standing right in front of us for what happened last year, we’ll treat it with the utmost respect it deserves and deliver a performance that can get us over the line”.

title: Sixmilebridge growth a boost for business – PJ Ryan
excerpt: PJ RYAN has been in business in Sixmilebridge for more than 35 years, seeing “massive growth” in the village’s population while running PJ Ryan Oil alongside a tractor and machinery operation.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Sixmilebridge growth a boost for business – PJ Ryan
body: PJ RYAN has been in business in Sixmilebridge for more than 35 years, seeing “massive growth” in the village’s population while running PJ Ryan Oil alongside a tractor and machinery operation.
As chairman of the Sixmilebridge Town Team, Ryan takes an active role in community development in the area and notes that The Bridge’s population has grown significantly in recent years.

“The population of Sixmilebridge has increased massively over the last few years. There are new housing estates constantly being built here, and that’s down to the fact that we have a massive sewage treatment plant here which was a great addition to the town. It was actually great for the people who put the treatment plant there a long number of years ago that they built it in such a way that it could accommodate a lot more population than they had at the time”, Ryan explains.
As part of this explosive growth, PJ Ryan Oil now serves customers in a 20 mile basis although Sixmilebridge itself still remains an important part of its customer base.

“We basically deal with households; there are quite a lot of houses in Sixmilebridge that use natural gas, but there are still a lot of older houses here”, Ryan outlines, in reference to houses operating on older home heating oil systems.

While the growth of the village has brought challenges, Ryan says the local business community continues to receive strong support from residents. “Local support is very good and it’s a very good town to do business in; people are very loyal and they support all the local businesses”.

Although based in Sixmilebridge for more than 30 years, Ryan is a proud Cratloe man and highlights that a healthy sporting rivalry is good for business. “Sometimes that's not easy because the GAA is extremely strong and there's always a bit of rivalry. Sometimes I get in at the butt of that but it’s good fun, it is an extremely good village to do business in”, the heating oil supplier adds.

As chairman of the Sixmilebridge Town Team, Ryan is constantly endeavouring to improve infrastructure in the village and surrounding area, including a new footpath and traffic management system. On these measures, Ryan states that “This is very important because the volume of traffic around the village is huge compared to what was there. If you take it that there were only 1600 people in Sixmilebridge in 1986 compared to the six or seven thousand that’s there now”, highlighting the increased pressures on the community.
Road infrastructure is another concern, with the oil merchant arguing that upgrades are needed to deal with the changing demands placed on the village.

“We definitely need an upgrade in the roads. I suppose that brings problems as well, when you upgrade, it creates another problem because the speed of the traffic going through the village is very high. That was one of the things highlighted for us when we started the town team, the first thing mentioned was the speed of the traffic”.

title: LADIES FOOTBALL: Favourites Kilmihil, Kilmurry Ibrickane & Banner begin with wins & Liscannor shock Burren Gaels
excerpt: FAVOURITES Kilmihil, Kilmurry Ibrickane and Banner Ladies all began their Clare LGFA senior championship bids with winning starts while Liscannor reigned supreme over Burren Gaels to mark a successful jump to senior.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: LADIES FOOTBALL: Favourites Kilmihil, Kilmurry Ibrickane & Banner begin with wins & Liscannor shock Burren Gaels
body: FAVOURITES Kilmihil, Kilmurry Ibrickane and Banner Ladies all began their Clare LGFA senior championship bids with winning starts while Liscannor reigned supreme over Burren Gaels to mark a successful jump to senior.
Kilmurry Ibrickane accounting for Doora/Barefield may not have been a surprise but the twenty one point hammering dished out to The Parish certainly raised eyebrows.

Champions Kilmihil ran out convincing twenty eight point victors against Éire Óg which already ties up their clash with Kilmurry Ibrickane as one to decide who tops the group while the meeting of neighbours St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield and Éire Óg will determine who is battling relegation.
Back with a vengeance, Banner Ladies proved too strong for Fergus Rovers while the shock of the round saw Liscannor overturn Burren Gaels.

Round two takes place this Sunday. Doora/Barefield have had to concede home advantage and face Kilmihil at St Michael’s Park (15:30) while Kilmurry Ibrickane will look to record back to back wins at Éire Óg’s expense in Ennis (14:00).
In Group 2, the two defeated sides, Fergus Rovers face off with Burren Gaels in Páirc na Muintire, Lissycasey (13:30) while Banner Ladies head north to Liscannor at 14:00.
Kilmihil 5-21 Éire Óg 0-8 Venue: St Michael’s Park, Kilmihil
As expected Kilmihil kicked off the defence of their county title with victory against Éire Óg which already puts them in a firm position of advancing to the knockout stages.

Caught on their own kickouts on too many occasions, Éire Óg afforded Kilmihil opportunities to punish them which they duly did, seven of their sixteen points in the opening half stemming from turnovers from kickouts.
When the second half came around, Kilmihil turned their focus to green flags and they raided for four in the final quarter to flesh out the scoreline to twenty eight points by the final whistle.
Éire Óg missed their first two chances on goal, a wide and the crossbar denying Alanna McNamara who would be their chief scoring target over the hour.

Two goal opportunities were spurned by Kilmihil in the first quarter but they were raising white flags, Áine McNamara with a brace and Ailish Considine kicking a two pointer to respond to Alanna McNamara’s first point.
Considine’s quick thinking saw her go short with a 45 which allowed Katie Mullen to split the posts, this arriving after Considine had landed a second two pointer of the day on sixteen minutes.

As they began to struggle on kickouts, Éire Óg compounded matters by conceding frees which a clinical Kilmihil punished. They scored 0-7 without reply in the second quarter and by half time were 1-16 0-2 in front, the goal arriving on thirty minutes when Áine McNamara and Eimear Considine combined with a running attack for the experienced Eimear to finish to the net.

Playing with the aid of the breeze in the second half, Éire Óg brought more energy and pushed up on the Kilmihil kickout. They worked the ball to Alanna McNamara and scored on their first attack, they followed this with Sarah Redmond splitting the posts after driving forward from a solo and go. McNamara kicked the next two scores to see the Ennis side put four scores on the bounce.

Becky Mahon kicked Kilmihil’s first score of the half on thirty nine minutes and they added to this with an Ailish Considine free. Éire Óg replied with two scores in succession, Maggie Power and McNamara on target as the game entered the final quarter.

This became Kilmihil’s purple patch, Éire Óg’s decision to push up left them exposed at the back and the West Clare side capitalised. Edel McNamara hit the net in a move made by Eimear Considine on forty six minutes, she had a second on fifty five minutes, Considine again the provider via a solo and go fifty yards out before popping to Edel.

Possession stayed with Kilmihil, Katie Mullen finished goal number in their next attack, Eimear Considine again teeing up the shot. Considine took the credit for their fifth goal, her sister Ailish the provider in this instance.

title: Knockout stages await Kilmurry Ibrickane after breezing past Lissycasey
excerpt: KILMURRY IBRICKANE are the first side assured of a place in the knockout stages of the TUS Clare SFC after dismantling Lissycasey in comprehensive fashion.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Knockout stages await Kilmurry Ibrickane after breezing past Lissycasey
body: KILMURRY IBRICKANE are the first side assured of a place in the knockout stages of the TUS Clare SFC after dismantling Lissycasey in comprehensive fashion.
Kilmurry Ibrickane 1-16 Lissycasey 0-12 Venue: Zimmer Biomet Páirc Chíosóg, Ennis

Back to back wins have Kilmurry Ibrickane sitting top of Group 3 in the Clare SFC and on their way to the knockout stages. They kicked 1-7 without reply while limiting Lissycasey to just two points in the second half. At the very least, it will be a preliminary quarter-final for the Bricks, a scenario that only becomes possible if Corofin win both of their two remaining games and Lissycasey defeat St Breckans in the final round and only then it would be via scoring difference but they remain in a healthy spot in this regard.
This was a fixture with the potential to be the best of the six senior games in round two but it sadly didn’t live up to expectation.

For the second game in a row, Lissycasey were punished when they failed to win their kickout or the subsequent breaking ball. What will frustrate them even more is they lacked aggression and bite which was particularly obvious when the game was slipping from their hands at a rapid pace.

Victorious in both of their championship outings, Kilmurry Ibrickane have conceded a total of ten two pointers thus far, six against St Breckans and four to Lissycasey. They have maintained clean sheets in both games but will certainly look to cut back on the concession of two pointers.

Evan Cahill’s showing at midfield was a real plus for the Bricks. He was dominant in the air but offered a real atrong attacking presence when taking on the opposing defence and is giving a glimpse of what he can offer when breaking the lines to create scoring opportunities for himself and others.

Daniel Walsh has delivered solid performances in both games for Enda Coughlan’s side and chipped in with 1-1 in an attacking wing back role. The goal on thirty seven minutes arriving after Joshua Moloney cleaned up the break from a Kilmurry Ibrickane kickout, fed the ball to Cathal Talty who was composed in possession before offloading to the on-rushing Walsh.

This goal gave them the lead for the second time in the game, pushing them 1-9 0-11 clear and they never looked back. In fact, they went from strength to strength, kicking an unanswered 1-7 as Lissycasey were unable to respond to the green flag.

It was Walsh that kicked the first score of the evening, Moloney again having an involvement. Lissycasey replied in this instance with a brace of Daire Culligan two pointers, one from a free and the other from play arriving straight from the kickout as the ball went directly to Diarmuid McMahon who played it to Culligan.

By half time, it was six scores apiece but four of these for Lissycasey were two pointers. Ben Skeritt and Connor Meaney raising orange flags. With the breeze in their favour, Lissycasey needed to be more than four points ahead. They led by five on two different occasions but for the possession they had, the margin should have been extended.

On the restart, Kilmurry Ibrickane wasted no time in clawing into the deficit. Conor Burke fired over a two pointer with the half less than fifty seconds old, Dermot Coughlan then opened his account with a 45 and the gap was down to one.

A breach by Kilmurry Ibrickane allowed Conor Finnucane the chance to make it a two point game and he duly obliged but then Coughlan’s charges fired their 1-7 tally, Walsh raiding for goal with a double from Keelan Sexton, Dermot adding his second 45, Burke doubled his tally with Daryn Callinan kicking a two pointer and a point from play.

Their return of 1-7 arrived in a fourteen minute window, enabled by how they took control of Lissycasey restarts and aided by the lack of energy and fight from the Cusack Cup champions in the middle sector. The Bricks would go the final six minutes of normal time and entirety of additional time (three minutes) without a score.

Cahill was the standout for Kilmurry Ibrickane with Daniel Walsh, Joshua Moloney, Darragh Sexton and Cathal Talty also prominent. Even though they won by a margin of seven points, it’s far from the complete performance from the sixteen-time champions which is definitely a positive complaint when they have two wins from two.

Tactically the decision of David Considine and his management to assign Connor Meaney to centre forward to man-mark Dermot Coughlan, the conductor of the Kilmurry Ibrickane choir, worked in that it nullified the influence of their playmaker whose runs from deep are at the heartbeat of the Bricks at the best. They got this right but for the second game running found themselves obliterated in the second half on their own kickout and the breaks from it. The loss of Mikey O’Neill was felt here as he is well able to tidy breaks but they need to get stronger in this sector if they want to make the business end of the championship. They had too many players that were only lively in fits and spurts.

Regardless of how Corofin versus vs St Breckans pans out on Sunday, Lissycasey now need a final round win to secure a quarter-final berth, they’ll be facing the men from the Spa and will be treating it as a knockout tie.

title: Miltown look to continue moving in right direction & towards knockout stages
excerpt: ST JOSEPH’S MILTOWN manager Sean O’Brien believes his side are moving in the right direction.
author: Gearóid Howley
alt: Miltown look to continue moving in right direction & towards knockout stages
body: ST JOSEPH’S MILTOWN manager Sean O’Brien believes his side are moving in the right direction.
A hard-earned win over Doonbeg where they recovered from a three point deficit at half time to win by six has put them on the right path towards qualifying for the knockout stages of the Clare SFC.

Manager O’Brien was pleased with a lot of aspects from their first round win where they picked up a valuable two points. “It’s good to get points on the board on the first day out. I’m happy with how we played, I was happy with how we played in the first half as well, the ball just didn’t break our way. We got going there in the second half and made the most of it to get the two points.”

Cian Mahony proved the difference-maker after the interval, producing a superb individual display as he amassed 0-11, including two superb two-pointers that helped Miltown begin to build their momentum. “We want Cian to take on shots like that, he’s a brilliant shooter. We’ve several lads that can kick them so today was Mahony’s day”.

Cormac Murray’s injury-time goal appeared to put the result beyond doubt by stretching the margin to seven points, although Doonbeg responded with a late consolation green flag of their own. “It was needed because they went up and got a goal themselves,” O’Brien said. “We felt we got a good goal there. We had another one really well worked earlier in the game but just didn’t get the rub of the green when it wasn’t allowed to stand. We’re happy to get the goal and the two-pointer at the end”.

Round two pits them against Colm Collins’ Cratloe before the county champions Éire Óg await in the final round. “It’s as tough as it gets now against the two most recent teams to win it out. We’re happy with how we’re going too, we’ve made some positive steps and today was just another step on the road”.

title: Town Team are 'the voice of the people' in Sixmilebridge
excerpt: “THE voice of the people”, expressed through its Town Team is key to making Sixmilebridge such a strong community says Company Secretary Colette Myler.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Town Team are 'the voice of the people' in Sixmilebridge
body: “THE voice of the people”, expressed through its Town Team is key to making Sixmilebridge such a strong community says Company Secretary Colette Myler.
Originally from Dublin, Colette moved to the area in 2020 and recently sat down with The Clare Echo to discuss the Town Team’s role in shaping one of Clare’s most vibrant communities.

On how she came to be involved with the Town Team, Colette says that before she fully moved down she “was around the area and noticed a questionnaire in a local pub about what the town would like to see happening and what improvements they wanted. I actually filled it out and when they started to form the town team in 2023, I thought I’d get involved”, the Dublin native explains.

“My background is that I worked at the National Rehabilitation Hospital in Dun Laoghaire, which deals with spinal injuries, amputees, and brain injuries and rehabilitation after tragic accidents or complicated medical surgeries. I am an Access Auditor and I realised that my passion is to be part of whatever changes happen in the town, I really want to have some say in accessibility”. Colette went on to volunteer for the role of company secretary with the Town Team and has worked in the role ever since.

The Town Team works on a monthly basis to progress its masterplan. The masterplan (Sixmilebridge Town Centre First Plan, June 2023) was funded by Clare County Council and collated with extensive input from the people of Sixmilebridge Town itself. The Town Team is the voice of the community works in partnership with Clare County Council through its Town Centre First Team and the Shannon Municipal District. As an administrator with the Town Team, Colette highlights that “If small groups in the town don't have the capacity to go for grants or projects, they can come to us and we should be helping them”. Projects do need to fall under one of the master plan’s documented goals.

The people of The Bridge are renowned for their hard work in achieving the best for their area, something which Colette notes helps to make the town a better place. “The people I'm involved with are very passionate about wanting to see the town improve for the greater good of the people. They want the best for the area. It shouldn't ever just be the majority shouting; we have to see the minorities as well and try to support them too”.

“There are a number of people on the Town Team that identify that need; they just love the place and are passionate about it. They are upset when they see negative behaviour, but they want to do something about it rather than sitting back and letting it happen. We also have a fabulous Sixmilebridge Community Development Association (SCDA/Tidy Towns) with people doing amazing work that a lot of the town’s people don't realise. The town looks fantastic because of their efforts and the significant group of people that actually come out to work on it”, she continues.

Despite only residing in The Bridge for a relatively short amount of time, Colette has noticed a number of changes in the town. Sixmilebridge has seen a number of large scale housing developments in recent years as well as improvements to its rail service, the only active station outside of Ennis in the county.

Since the Town Team’s official incorporation in 2024, Colette’s proudest achievement with the group is the main committee’s excellent working relationship. The committee of circa 19 to 23 members is crucial in achieving the best for Sixmilebridge. “The people around the table are vital. What’s really important to me is that when they come, they actively participate What we need more than anything else is the voice of the people at the table”, the Access Auditor outlines.

On a positive note, Colette advised that the Town Team with Clare County Council is actively engaged in plans for a Park-for-All. There is much work to be done on this project, including community engagement, however there is a hard working local community project team steering the proposal. Colette added that it will be a huge asset for the wellbeing of the town when it is realised.

title: Cratloe in must-win territory but McInerney return not expected until 'latter stages'
excerpt: CRATLOE’s senior footballers are in “must-win” territory following their “comprehensive” drubbing to champions Éire Óg in round one.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Cratloe in must-win territory but McInerney return not expected until 'latter stages'
body: CRATLOE’s senior footballers are in “must-win” territory following their “comprehensive” drubbing to champions Éire Óg in round one.

Three teams will emerge from the seeded Group 1 to make the Clare SFC quarter-finals meaning Cratloe need to get points on the board this Saturday when they face St Joseph’s Miltown in Páirc Finne (17:00).

For Cratloe, a huge improvement is needed following their 1-17 0-4 loss to Éire Óg a fortnight ago. “We knew we were in trouble but I didn’t think it would be as comprehensive as that. Fair play to Éire Óg, they were very clinical, every chance and turnover they punished us so credit to them, a good win for them but we have to regroup and try our best to put in a performance the next day,” manager Colm Collins told The Clare Echo.

In his twenty year stint in charge of the Cratloe footballers, the hour on the sideline watching Éire Óg ease past them was among the longest hours that Collins endured. “I knew we were in trouble, we were down five starting players, you don’t replace five starting players too easily. With the format of the championship now, if a fella gets injured now he could miss the whole thing, we’ll see how we go, hopefully we’ll have a few back in two weeks time and put in a better performance”.

Páirc Finne was the setting when Cratloe defeated Ennistymon in extra time in last year’s quarter-final, they return to Corofin now seeking to revive their chances of reaching the knockout stages. “We must win from now on, there’s no messing about it, concentration now is our next game against Miltown and putting in a good performance, that is it and that is all we can do”
Hindering their cause against Éire Óg was the absence of Podge Collins (hamstring), Rian Considine (groin), Cathal McInerney (calf), Tadhg Lohan (hand) and David Collins (hamstring).

Both Podge and Rian returned to action for the Cratloe hurlers in their second round draw with O’Callaghans Mills last Saturday but the timeframe for McInerney and Lohan is a bit longer. “David is nearly there, Tadhg Lohan will be a couple more weeks and I’d say it will be the latter stages of the championship before we have Cathal back,” Collins confirmed.

title: Young Kilkee entrepreneur cracks the secret to egg business
excerpt: A YOUNG Kilkee entrepreneur is hatching a growing business in Moveen, going from two hens to a flock of 98 to keep his honesty box at the cliffs stocked.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Young Kilkee entrepreneur cracks the secret to egg business
body: A YOUNG Kilkee entrepreneur is hatching a growing business in Moveen, going from two hens to a flock of 98 to keep his honesty box at the cliffs stocked.

Ubh by Paudie is a fast growing enterprise with the nine year old CEO restocking his honesty box daily at 2pm as well as managing his busy social media which currently boasts over 23,000 followers on Instagram.

“I wanted two goldfish and we got two chickens instead because my dad eats eggs every morning. You can pet the hens but you can’t pet goldfish”, the young entrepreneur explained. The idea developed into a small egg-selling business, with Paudie initially selling the eggs from his family home before setting up the egg box close to Goleen Bay in the far west of the County.

The venture began over the June Bank Holiday weekend and has been a whirlwind success ever since. On the profits he makes, Paudie demonstrates a good head for business, saying “I invest it back into the business and buy more hens”, reinvesting his earnings to expand his flock.
Running a business comes with plenty of responsibility as Paudie begins each day early to make sure that his prized hens are properly cared for.

“I get up around six in the morning. I go up and give them fresh water, fresh feed, fresh straw”, the Moveen man explained. The honesty box has become a huge hit on social media with tourists to the area from as far away as Pennsylvania adding Ubh by Paudie to their itinerary.
While social media can often be unpredictable, Paudie is confident that interest in the egg box will continue. “I know that it won’t drop off. I’m almost positive. 100%,” he said.
With the new school year fast approaching, Paudie is unfazed by the challenge of balancing his schoolwork with his daily responsibilities of looking after the hens and keeping the egg box stocked.
“My loving father will do it for me”, he jokes, confident that his budding enterprise will continue to grow over the coming months.
For now, Paudie is content to keep learning the ropes of the business one egg at a time and with his flock increasing all the time, his little enterprise could soon be getting a whole lot bigger.

title: Méabh, Mark & Shane to fly the Clare flag at Rose of Tralee
excerpt: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s Méabh Holland is bidding to become only the second Clare woman to win the Rose of Tralee while two Clare men will serve as escorts for the famed festival.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Méabh, Mark & Shane to fly the Clare flag at Rose of Tralee
body: SIXMILEBRIDGE’s Méabh Holland is bidding to become only the second Clare woman to win the Rose of Tralee while two Clare men will serve as escorts for the famed festival.
Tralee welcomes the Roses and Escorts for the 67th festival with the Sixmilebridge woman an outside contender to be named the Rose of Tralee.
Twenty two year old Méabh was selected as the Clare Rose at the beginning of May, prevailing in a contest of fourteen to succeed Feakle’s Aisling O’Connor who made it to the Dome in August 2023.

A primary school teacher, Méabh has a love for her native language and spent her summers teaching Gaeilge in Connemara. She teaches the concertina with Music Generation Clare and The Irish Concertina Orchestra.

Ladbrokes have Méabh at 25/1 to win outright. Nicola McGeady of Ladbrokes commented, “Clare have only won the competition once, almost 60 years ago. However, Clare locals are backing their Rose to go all the way this year”.
Adding to the Clare contingent in Tralee are escorts, Shane Harrison from Quin and Barefield’s Mark Lynch.

Twenty four year old Shane is a graduate of the University of Limerick who now works as a site engineer in Galway. “Home has always been a huge part of who I am. Growing up in Clare has given me a great appreciation for community, and I've been fortunate to spend most of my life playing hurling with Clooney/Quin GAA Club. Whether I'm on the pitch, helping out on the farm, or catching up with family and friends, I'm happiest when I'm surrounded by good people,” he said.

“Away from work, I love music, travelling, and experiencing new places and cultures. One of my biggest goals is to visit as many countries as I can. I enjoy making the most of every opportunity, having a laugh, and never saying no to a new adventure. I'm really looking forward to the Rose of Tralee Festival as I think It's a fantastic opportunity to meet people from all over the world and make lifelong memories. Most of all, I'm excited to embrace the experience and have plenty of craic along the way,” Shane added.
A pharmacist at Marry Jo Duffy’s in Ennis, Mark quipped that he spends his working hours “reading impossible penmanship and gently explaining that antibiotics won't cure a hangover”.

There will be a strong Clare spirit in Tralee, the twenty nine year old outlined, “Outside the pharmacy, I'm a massive fan of Clare GAA and Munster Rugby, and can usually otherwise be found at a music festival or concert. Growing up with a younger sister and working almost exclusively with women, I consider myself a master in the art of patience, a trait that will come in remarkably handy in Tralee. I'm swapping the dispensary for the Dome to bring proper Banner spirit to Kerry and ensure my Rose has an absolute blast, while entertaining with my impressions and dry wit”.
The Rose of Tralee airs on RTÉ One and RTÉ Player on Monday 17 August and Tuesday 18 August from 8pm.

title: Uisce Éireann urges Clare people to conserve water amid ongoing dry weather
excerpt: UISCE Éireann is urging people in Clare to continue conserving water as supplies remain under pressure amid ongoing warm and dry conditions.
author: Paige Foley
alt: Uisce Éireann urges Clare people to conserve water amid ongoing dry weather
body: UISCE Éireann is urging people in Clare to continue conserving water as supplies remain under pressure amid ongoing warm and dry conditions.
Water supplies are being closely monitored in the county, with tankering operations ongoing in Carran and Crusheen.
A nationwide Water Conservation Order remains in place until August 26 following a prolonged period of exceptionally warm and dry weather, combined with high demand for water.
Uisce Éireann said conservation efforts by customers have helped to reduce demand in many areas, but several water sources remain under pressure.
The appeal comes as Met Éireann has issued a Status Yellow High Temperature Warning for parts of the country, with higher temperatures expected to increase demand for water in the coming days.
Uisce Éireann Operations Manager Darragh Conneely said customers' efforts to conserve water were helping to protect supplies.
“However, many of our water sources remain under pressure following an extended period of warm and dry weather and it will take time for those sources to recover,” he said.
“With warm conditions expected to continue and temperatures set to rise again in parts of the country, we are asking everyone to continue doing what they can to conserve water.”

People are being asked to avoid non-essential water use and to take simple steps such as taking shorter showers, fixing leaking taps and toilets, fully loading dishwashers and washing machines, and using a watering can instead of a hose or sprinkler.
Uisce Éireann said it is also taking measures to protect supplies, including maximising water production, repairing leaks and managing network pressures.
The Water Conservation Order is being reviewed on an ongoing basis, taking into account weather conditions, soil moisture deficits and the status of water supplies.
People can find practical water-saving advice at water.ie/conservation and can report leaks on the public network by calling 1800 278 278.

title: ‘Absolutely no excuse’ – Clare cllr condemns illegal dumping at Mooghaun Forest
excerpt: A CLARE cllr has strongly condemned a recent spate of illegal dumping reported at Mooghaun Forest, describing the incident as an unacceptable act that could damage the local environment.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: ‘Absolutely no excuse’ – Clare cllr condemns illegal dumping at Mooghaun Forest
body: A CLARE cllr has strongly condemned a recent spate of illegal dumping reported at Mooghaun Forest, describing the incident as an unacceptable act that could damage the local environment.
Cllr David Griffin (FF), spoke to The Clare Echo regarding the issue at the Newmarket On Fergus site which contains what is believed to be the largest evidence of a hill fort in Ireland.

One of the youngest elected representatives in the county, cllr Griffin highlighted that “Mooghaun Forest is an important local amenity, and it is disappointing to see it affected by illegal dumping. This type of dumping creates unnecessary work for those responsible for maintaining and improving the area”, the Newmarket man continued.
A large volume of discarded household and electrical waste was found at the site earlier this week along a popular walking route, known locally as The Long Sweep.

“Mooghaun Forest is a valuable natural space for local people, families, walkers, and visitors. It should be protected and respected, not subjected to this kind of reckless behaviour. We all have a responsibility to protect our natural environment”.

“There is absolutely no excuse for this type of behaviour, and I would encourage anyone who encounters illegal dumping anywhere in the County to ensure it is reported to Clare County Council's environment team”, Griffin added. The Fianna Fáil representative reminded people in Clare to contact the local authority’s Litter Helpline to report illegal dumping on 1800 606 706 or enviroff@clarecoco.ie.

The woods are situated on the grounds of Dromoland Castle, with remnants of the hill fort dating from the Bronze Age located nearby. A large hoard of Late Bronze Age jewellery was found at the site in 1854 during the construction of a railway line from Ennis to Limerick.

title: Doonbeg to tighten up on concession of 'detrimental' two-pointers
excerpt: BRIAN Shanahan lamented Doonbeg's concession of five second-half two-pointers when reflecting on their first round loss to St Joseph’s Miltown in the Clare SFC.
author: Gearóid Howley
alt: Doonbeg to tighten up on concession of 'detrimental' two-pointers
body: BRIAN Shanahan lamented Doonbeg's concession of five second-half two-pointers when reflecting on their first round loss to St Joseph’s Miltown in the Clare SFC.

Despite leading by three points at the interval, Doonbeg manager Brian Shanahan admitted his side's inability to contain Miltown's long-range threat proved decisive as they slipped to defeat in their opening Clare SFC outing.

“It was a game of two halves really. The first half we were very good. We won the first half, they won the second half, so basically their shots went over the bar and ours didn't. That was the story of the game really. They got five two-pointers, three of them were kind of given away from indiscipline, but there's a lot to build on for the next game,” he reflected.

Miltown overturned the deficit almost immediately after the restart, with Cian Mahony inspiring a blistering spell that saw the eventual winners race into a two-point lead inside the opening three minutes of the second half. “We went in at half-time three points up, two and a half minutes into the second half we were two points down. They scored five points there in the first two minutes and that's ultimately where the damage was done. We know the two-pointers are massive scores and, to be fair, he [Mahony] had his shooting boots on. When a forward is on form, he's on form. We didn't help ourselves standing off him”.

Although Cormac Murray's late goal added further gloss to the scoreboard, Shanahan felt the final six-point margin did not accurately reflect the contest. “I don't think they were six points better than us. Our shot selection was poor basically. We had nine very bad misses in the second half and there were easily two of those that were goal chances. A six-point loss wasn't a fair reflection on the game, I don't think,” he stated.

The Magpies now face reigning champions Éire Óg before a final-round meeting with Cratloe, with Shanahan viewing their round two clash is a free shot ahead of what he expects to be the decisive group fixture. “We have a free crack at Éire Óg now next, the result is irrelevant whether we win or lose. Ultimately it'll come down to the last game with Cratloe with three teams coming out of our group. We'll just try and improve things for Éire Óg. There'll be no pressure, it doesn't make a difference whether we win, lose or draw. It'll come down to that last game”.

title: Tuam marks 35 years of twinning partnership with German city Straubing
excerpt: Galway County Council Director of Services Michael Owens; Cathaoirleach of the Municipal District of Tuam Cllr Mary Hoade; and Lord Mayor of Straubing Markus Pannermayr pictured in Straubing, Germany.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Tuam marks 35 years of twinning partnership with German city Straubing
body: Galway County Council Director of Services Michael Owens; Cathaoirleach of the Municipal District of Tuam Cllr Mary Hoade; and Lord Mayor of Straubing Markus Pannermayr pictured in Straubing, Germany.
REPRESENTATIVES from Tuam are in Germany this week to celebrate the 35th anniversary of the town's twinning partnership with the Bavarian city of Straubing.

Cathaoirleach of the Municipal District of Tuam Cllr Mary Hoade (FF) is leading the delegation, accompanied by Galway County Council Director of Services Michael Owens and Meetings Administrator Geraldine Byrne.

The visit centres on a special Town Partnership Day, bringing together delegations from Straubing's three twinned towns, Tuam, Romans in France and Wels in Austria, to celebrate more than three decades of European friendship and cooperation.

The programme includes a civic reception, visits to major civic projects, discussions on international youth work, and participation in events at the Gäubodenvolksfest, one of Bavaria's largest traditional festivals, which attracts hundreds of thousands of visitors each year.

Also attending are Deputy Consul of Ireland in Munich Kate Hall and Tara Baynes from the Irish Consulate. The partnership dates back to the mid-1980s, when Tuam historian Dr Tony Claffey proposed a twinning based on the shared heritage and the cultural and religious links established by early Irish missionaries in Bavaria.

German was being taught in most Tuam secondary schools by 1987, with annual student exchanges beginning two years later. The twinning was formally ratified in 1991 and has since developed into a wide-ranging partnership encompassing education, culture, tourism and business. Exchanges have involved schools, music and theatre groups, while Tuam students have taken up summer employment in Straubing. The close relationship is also reflected in Straubing, where a street has been named in honour of Tuam.

Cllr Hoade said the 35th anniversary was an opportunity to recognise the generations who had built and maintained the relationship. “The 35th anniversary is a significant milestone for Tuam and Straubing. What began with our shared heritage and cultural connections has developed into a lasting friendship involving schools, community groups, businesses and families”.

She added, “The annual student exchanges, which began in 1989, are an important part of that relationship and have created friendships and connections that have lasted across generations. It is a great honour to represent Tuam in Straubing as we celebrate this important anniversary”.

Lord Mayor (Oberbürgermeister) of Straubing Markus Pannermayr said the partnership had created lasting links between the two communities. “For 35 years, Tuam and Straubing have built a partnership based on friendship, mutual respect and learning from each other. It has grown from its early focus on education into a wider relationship involving culture, music, business, tourism and community life. We are delighted to welcome our friends from Tuam this week and look forward to many more years of friendship and cooperation”.

Michael Owens, Director of Services with Galway County Council's Municipal District of Tuam, said the relationship had been sustained by generations of people in both communities. “The strength of the Tuam-Straubing relationship is that it has always been about people. Over 35 years, students, families, community groups, performers and businesses have maintained those links. The 35th anniversary is an opportunity to acknowledge everyone who has contributed to the partnership and to build on those connections for future generations”.

The historic city of Straubing in southeast Germany is located on the banks of the River Danube. With a population of around 50,000, it is known for its well-preserved medieval centre, Gothic architecture and strong agricultural heritage.

title: Moving round of Clare SFC will tell a lot as to Jack Daly contenders
excerpt: MOVING round of the Clare senior and intermediate football championships arrive this weekend where places in the knockout stages can be secured.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Moving round of Clare SFC will tell a lot as to Jack Daly contenders
body: MOVING round of the Clare senior and intermediate football championships arrive this weekend where places in the knockout stages can be secured.

There will be plenty of movement for supporters too as the decision of Clare GAA not to host a single double-header between senior and intermediate leaves patrons scrambling from venue to venue to try see games in the flesh.
Back to back victories will at the very least secure a spot in the preliminary quarter-finals whereas other sides that record successive wins will be able to look forward to the knockout stages.
On the flipside, following up a round one loss with another defeat in round two will move clubs closer to a relegation battle.
It won’t be until the final round in the group stages takes place in a fortnight that the standings in each group will be finalised.

Kicking off the action is the battle to top Group 3 when Kilmurry Ibrickane and Lissycasey face off in Cusack Park on Friday evening at 18:45. This could well be a pairing later on in the year with both sides capable of forging a successful run in the knockout stages. Whoever progresses is likely to top the group following their victories in round one.

Notably both sides saw extensive leads cut back to two points after conceding a brace of two pointers so they have plenty to learn heading into round two. Dermot Coughlan and Caoilfhionn O’Dea excelled for Kilmurry Ibrickane as they showed their ability to attack in numbers and at pace while Lissycasey brought an array of firepower up front with Daire Culligan, Shane Griffin, Conor Finnucane and Diarmuid McMahon to the fore.

Corofin and St Breckans will both be looking to bounce back in what is a novel North Clare derby on Sunday afternoon (15:00) in Gurteen. They last met in the 2022 champonship when the Spa prevailed 0-14 1-7. It will be even tighter this weekend with both sides knowing a win will bolster their chances of qualifying for a preliminary quarter-final if not the last eight. Diarmuid Cahill remains sidelined for Corofin but they will hope to have Damien O’Loughlin and Cilléin Mullins back in action. St Breckans apart from their two pointers lacked an attacking threat while their defence was ripped open by the Bricks so a big improvement is required by Patrick O’Neill’s side.

Champions Éire Óg can secure their spot in the quarter-finals if they overcome Doonbeg on Saturday (16:00) in Páirc na Muintire, Lissycasey. The Townies strolled past Cratloe 1-17 0-4 in round one while Doonbeg came close to upsetting St Joseph’s Miltown. Colm Walsh O’Loghlen continues his recovery from an ACL injury for Éire Óg who came through the second round of the Clare SHC without additional injuries, a red card for David McNamara a fortnight ago means they will be without his powerful presence in the middle third. Seán Conway may be pressing for inclusion to make a first championship start in two years for Doonbeg who will need Darragh Burns, Darragh O’Sullivan, David Tubridy, Tadhg Lillis and Mikie Tubridy on fire to take down the champions.

A second win for Seán O’Brien’s St Joseph’s Miltown would seal their progression to the quarter-finals. The West Clare side had an abundance of threats up front which helped them recover from a three point half-time deficit to beat Doonbeg 1-21 2-12. It can only get better for Cratloe following their first round no-show but they will welcome back Podge Collins and Rian Considine to their attack to increase the questions they will pose of opposing defences.

Last year’s beaten finalists St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield will endeavour to bring their campaign to life when they face off with Kildysart on Saturday (13:00) in Clarecastle. The sides finished all square at 1-12 apiece in the 2025 first round, scoring difference ultimately sending The Parish through and they backed it up with wins over Kilmurry Ibrickane and Cratloe to make a first county final since 2012. Kildysart had a nervy opening half against Kilmihil but they outscored their opponents 0-9 0-2 in the second half to take the points. Niall Ginnane’s side will look to put more points on the board to edge closer to the knockout stages.

Once bitten twice shy will be in the minds of Ennistymon as they face Kilmihil in round two for the second year in a row. Kilmihil had three points to spare over Ennistymon in one of the shocks of the season, this will give them great confidence of repeating the dose. Ennistymon rightly have ambitions of having a big say in where Jack Daly resides for the winter, a second win on the trot will move them towards an eleventh quarter-final in twelve seasons. Notably the tie throws up a double derby with former Kilmihil footballer Declan Downes in charge of Ennistymon while Denis Hynes, an Ennistymon native and coach of their senior side in 2021 part of the Kilmihil management.

title: Survival & success the focus as ten camogie clubs begin to move for McMahon Cup
excerpt: TEN teams take off in pursuit of the McMahon Cup with the Clare Credit Unions Senior Camogie Championship commencing this Friday.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Survival & success the focus as ten camogie clubs begin to move for McMahon Cup
body: TEN teams take off in pursuit of the McMahon Cup with the Clare Credit Unions Senior Camogie Championship commencing this Friday.
It’s Friday night lights across the county with four senior games down for decision.
With two teams getting relegated from the top tier this season, consolidation is as important as progression for all sides as they earmark starting with a win in round one.

Holders Inagh/Kilnamona will carry the favourites tag and will look to win back to back titles for the first time since 2018. Eugene Foudy has concluded his first season as Clare senior camogie manager but his focus is now solely on club matters. They will look to lay down a marker against reigning intermediate champions Clooney/Quin in round one. Clare Hehir, Andrea O’Keeffe, Aoife Keane, Sinead Power and Aoibhin Ryan will be central players during their run.

No better baptism of fire for Clooney/Quin than facing the county’s top team to see what level they are at. Eoin Gallagher has a youthful side at his disposal who will need to bring a no fear element if they are to match Inagh/Kilnamona in round one. Having won the intermediate title in 2021, Clooney/Quin made a swift drop back down to the second tier, avoiding a repeat scenario is the focus for the club who will be relying on Ciara Grogan, Emma Deegan, Emma Considine and the Halpin sisters.

Clarecastle/Ballyea are braced for a fourth successive senior at senior level. Though there would be a historic rivalry between the Magpies and Newmarket-on-Fergus, that has been non-existent in camogie. Continuity in terms of personnel on and off the field has been a challenge for Clarecastle/Ballyea over the last three seasons but they have edged all their focus on causing an upset in round one. Doireann Murphy who lines out in goals for her county, is likely to feature outfield for her club.

A decade has passed since Newmarket-on-Fergus last lifted the McMahon Cup. The aspirations of the club have shifted from a side regularly listed as contenders to an outfit now primarily focused on avoiding a relegation scrap. Three-time senior championship winner Geraldine O’Grady enters the hotseat as manager, she’s less vocal than her older sister Trish on the sideline but is looking to orchestrate the same results. Injury has ruled out last year’s captain Katie O’Flanagan for the season, the Blues are buoyed by their minor success a week ago. Finding the right mix between youth and experience is key, Michelle McMahon, Carol O’Leary, Caoimhe Lally, Ellen Casey, Kate Kennedy, Aoibhe O’Leary and Laura McMahon are important cogs in their wheel.

Every team has had a long wait for the championship to start but it is an extended period for Kilmaley who have a bye in round one. Shane Slattery remains in charge of the four-time champions who will field one of their stronger panels in recent times with Eimear Considine making a return to their panel. The McMahon sisters Claire and Helen remain from their championship winning sides with Sinead O’Keeffe, Caoimhe Carmody and Regan Conway adding energy across the field.

Pain of last year’s extra time final defeat to Inagh/Kilnamona has left a sting in the tail for Truagh/Clonlara who were edged out in their efforts to win three successive senior titles. It’s back to the drawing board and a new campaign but the South-East Clare side will be one of the fancied sides to be in the knockout stages. Injuries have deprived them of key players over the past two seasons but it’s a full hand to pick from for Bob Caulfield and his management which this year includes ex Parteen/Meelick manager Denis Barry. Eimear Kelly, Roisin Begley, Laura Foley and Áine O’Loughlin will cause problems for any opposing side in Group 2.

Feakle/Killanena’s cause has been dealt a major blow with the loss of Lorna McNamara. Having been in the form that had her a shoe-in for an All Star nomination, the Clare taliswoman suffered a devastating ACL injury which will leave her sidelined for club action this season. It will hamper their chances of making it beyond the semi-final stages once again. To even reach that juncture, they’ll need to take down either of East Clare’s big two, Truagh/Clonlara or Scariff/Ogonnelloe.

Retaining senior status was the big focus for Tulla when making the jump last year, it’s a new year but the objective remains the same. They’ll potentially eye up their third round with St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield as a county final to determine who may drop down but the side managed by two-time Clare SHC winner Johnny Brigdale from Crusheen won’t take a step back from any of their other opponents in Group 2.

If ever there was a sign that Scariff/Ogonnelloe mean business, bringing back Lorrha native David Sullivan as manager is as clear as it gets. He led them to county and provincial glory in 2021 but left in sudden circumstances the following spring. The experienced Mairead Scanlan returns to the panel with the McGee sisters while ex Clare defender Amy Barrett is gone from the squad. They are in action for four weeks on the trot so they’ll aim to have their statements made and place in the semi-finals secured by then. Abby Walsh, Aoife Power, Alva Rodgers and Roisin Minogue will be among those leading the way.

Watching from the sidelines this weekend is St Joseph’s Doora/Barefield who have the bye in Group 2. After their ladies footballers slumped to a disappointing first round hammering, the Parish will be hopeful that their camogie side can offer a lift when their campaign springs to life on Friday week. They made the Senior B final last season and will look to be back at that same stage, this will only be possible if they maintain their status.

title: Scariff Bay Community Radio seek support for church-gate collection
excerpt: SCARIFF BAY Community Radio (SBCR) will be holding their annual church gate collection this weekend across East Clare.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: Scariff Bay Community Radio seek support for church-gate collection
body: SCARIFF BAY Community Radio (SBCR) will be holding their annual church gate collection this weekend across East Clare.
Before all masses in the East Clare area, SBCR will be collecting money as part of their annual church gate collection on Saturday August 15th and Sunday August 16th.
“Your contribution would be appreciated as it is a voluntary service,” Chairman of SBCR Pat O’Brien said when appealing to the public to support their continued fundraising efforts.

Last month, SBCR claimed gold at the Craol annnual achievement awards winning top accolades for programming from Scoil Samhraidh Willie Clancy, promotion of the Irish language and in-depth feature on domestic abuse.
In December, SBCR was awarded a ten-year broadcasting licence by Coimisiún na Meán. It is the first time that the community radio station signed a full-time broadcasting contract.
Run by volunteers, SBCR is also set to enter into a partnership with Clare County Council to operate their new podcast studio in the Scariff hub.

title: Caherhurley Plant Nursery back to full strength after owner's health scare
excerpt: CAHERHURLEY Organic Nursery in Bodyke has fully reopened to the public with opening hours of 9am to 5pm seven days a week.
author: Michael Fitzgerald
alt: Caherhurley Plant Nursery back to full strength after owner's health scare
body: CAHERHURLEY Organic Nursery in Bodyke has fully reopened to the public with opening hours of 9am to 5pm seven days a week.
After a turbulent time for Gert, the owner, his health issues are resolving and Caherhurley is back on its feet again.
The nursey has improved, thanks to the help of volunteers, trainees and students of horticultural colleges.

Caherhurley Nursery is a place where gardeners love to go for their plants, because it's exceptional in many ways: It's a nursery where plants are slowly grown outside on a windy hillside, without artificial fertilisers to ensure that they are hardy and they can survive the challenging, harsh Irish climate.
Once they grow there, they will survive anywhere. Also, the plants are certified organic, that's the only guarantee that no bee-killing chemicals were used.
A wide range of unusual herbaceous hardy perennials are grown, offering something else then what's generally available.

Plants are propagated by the growers themselves and produced in the nursery, nothing is bought in. In this respect, Caherhurley Nursery is unique because most Irish nurseries grow plants that are imported as young plants from abroad.

According to the team at Caherhurley, “People find it refreshing to buy from a nursery where they can get expert advise on the choices of their plants and it's great to see how they are propagated and grown”.
All are welcome to visit Caherhurley Organic Nursery in Bodyke at V94K3E or online at www.caherhurleynursery.com.

title: €25m in damages awarded to family of Lahinch's Micheál 'Mick' Ryan in landmark case against Boeing
excerpt: FAMILY of the late Lahinch native Micheál ‘Mick’ Ryan have been awarded $29m (€25m) in damages from Boeing.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: €25m in damages awarded to family of Lahinch's Micheál 'Mick' Ryan in landmark case against Boeing
body: FAMILY of the late Lahinch native Micheál ‘Mick’ Ryan have been awarded $29m (€25m) in damages from Boeing.
In December 2021, Mick’s wife Naoise Connolly Ryan filed a US court motion over the February 2019 Boeing 737 MAX crash which claimed Mick’s life and that of all 157 people on board.
A Chicago jury awarded $29 million (€25 million) in damages to Mick’s family.
Father of two Mick was one of the final remaining civil suits pending against Boeing following the pair of deadly MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019 that together claimed 346 lives.

The vast majority of claims have been settled out of court with undisclosed terms, but Ms Connolly Ryan's attorney Steven Marks had described his client as “committed to seeking accountability and justice from a jury and not accepting money from Boeing directly”.

An offer of $1.4m made from the crash victim fund was previously rejected by Naoise. She stated in December 2021, “It’s blood money. This isn’t about money. I say this all the time, it’s about truth, accountability, and real justice”.

Boeing has apologised for the crashes and acknowledged that anti-stall software was implicated in both incidents. In May, a Chicago jury awarded $49.5m in damages to the family of Samya Stumo, a 24-year-old American who was killed on the same flight.

The 157 victims included people from 35 countries. The flight, which was bound for the Kenyan capital of Nairobi, came down near the town of Bishoftu, 50km southeast of Addis Abada. The jet left the airport at 8.38am local time on 10 March 2019 before losing contact with the control tower at 8.44am. The airline's chief executive said the pilot, who had an “excellent flying record”, reported difficulties and had been cleared to turn back. The aircraft was just a few months old, having taken its first flight at the end of October. Its last maintenance was on 4 February 2019 and it had flown just 1,200 hours.

Aged 39 at the time of his death, Mick was a senior humanitarian worker with the United Nations. He dedicated his life to humanitarian work overseas helping people in need in Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, Ethiopia, Liberia, and the world’s largest refugee camp in Myanmar. Mick worked as the deputy chief engineer with the United Nations World Food Programme.

From Attychristoria in Lahinch, Mick lived with his wife and children in Cork City. He had been based in the Rome headquarters of the UN World Food Programme and the family were due to relocate to Italy in March 2019. He is the son of Christina a retired teacher at Scoil Mhuire, Ennistymon and Jack an accountant who died in 2013 and a brother of Cristin, Siobhan and Tiernan.
In 2020, Mick was posthumously named the Humanitarian of the Year by the Irish Red Cross.

title: 'We'll be tested in every game of the Clare SFC' insists Éire Óg boss Daniels
excerpt: DESPITE strolling to a seventeen point victory in round one, Éire Óg manager Shane Daniels insisted they were tested as they brushed by the challenge of Cratloe.
author: Páraic McMahon
alt: 'We'll be tested in every game of the Clare SFC' insists Éire Óg boss Daniels
body: DESPITE strolling to a seventeen point victory in round one, Éire Óg manager Shane Daniels insisted they were tested as they brushed by the challenge of Cratloe.
Each outing in the Clare SFC provides stiff tests, Éire Óg manager Daniels stressed following their comprehensive start to defending their title as county champions.

He told The Clare Echo, “Every day you go out you try work on a couple of things, we worked on a couple again It was a test, Cratloe battled hard, they didn’t get the scores on the board, they were missing a couple of players but every game you go out in Clare in the senior football championship you get tested, we were happy with aspects of what we were working on and disappointed with aspects too”.

They had two debutants in round one, teenager Danny Lyne making his bow at corner forward while three-time All-Ireland senior club winner with Galway club, Benard Power made his debut between the posts. “Bernard has been around a while, he is a really good goalkeeper, he is a great addition to the squad and we’re very happy with his performance,” said the five-time Clare SFC winner.

Shane continued, “Every day you go you you’re hoping you don’t get injuries, we can get injuries when we’re training for football next week, we’re trying to build a panel so if guys do pick up injuries we have guys to come in. Danny Lyne started today, his first start and he is only out of minor, I thought he did quite well, worked really hard and got a point on the board, he will be a super footballer as he goes on, so we’re just hoping to keep building”.

“We’ve lots to work on, we’re getting some young fellas into the team, we have to try integrate them in. Can we do our transition better when we’re moving the ball, can we do it faster, we have loads to work on. We asked for a bit of honesty and workrate from the lads and in fairness this group always do that,” he added.

Introduced off the bench for the first time in championship was David Loftus while Jack Joyce landed a two pointer when he entered the fray. “Jack Joyce is a super footballer, he could be playing the next game, that is just the way it is, we’re trying to build a squad and do the right thing, we’re trying to get competition for places and that is one thing we have, we had an inter-county footballer coming off the bench, we had Jack Joyce too, Jarlath Collins a super footballer, we brought on another young fella David Loftus who has a big future too”.

Within defence, Ronan Lanigan lined out at centre back and anchored their backline well. “Ronan Lanigan is a super footballer, he can play in any position, you can play him in any of the six backs or six forwards, he is a key player for us and we want him in a key position”.

David McNamara’s red card for an off the ball incident with Enda Boyce means the Townies are without his strong presence in the middle third for round two against Doonbeg. “I missed exactly what happened, we will look back at the video and see, if he was wrong and he get a red card then he was wrong, we’ll take it on the chin and move on”.

On the test that Doonbeg will pose, Shane stated, “Every game we play is going to be tough, every game is going to be a battle, it will be different to the Cratloe game but we’re ready for challenges, that is what we want”.
